The default truncate(16) keeps a 16-character prefix of string bounds, rounding a truncated upper bound up so that it still covers every value. Bounds are stored as bytes in a standard single-value form, because one manifest schema must hold any column type. For wide tables, metrics are inferred only for the first 100 columns. More statistics prune better but enlarge manifests and slow planning. Set full or another mode per column where it matters, for example an identifier whose first 16 characters are identical everywhere; the change affects only new files. Even good bounds skip nothing if every file spans the whole range, which sorting fixes. ALTER TABLE demo.shop.orders SET TBLPROPERTIES ( 'write.metadata.metrics.column.status' = 'full'); 28. Why are column renames safe? Column renames are safe because every field has a permanent ID and data files record those IDs. A rename changes only the name attached to an ID. Readers match columns by ID, including struct fields, list elements and map keys and values. An ID is never reused, so a column dropped and added again under the same name is a new column: current queries read null for older rows, while time travel to an earlier snapshot still shows the old values under that snapshot’s schema. Formats that match by name can expose old data when a name is reused, and formats that match by position shift columns when one is dropped. Files written outside Iceberg carry no IDs, so a name mapping in schema.name-mapping.default tells readers which names correspond to which IDs. Migration procedures set it up, and if you later rename such a column, keep the old name in the mapping. A rename edits the schema, not the files. 29. Which type promotions are allowed? Iceberg allows only widening type changes, ones that can still read every old value exactly. The table below lists them with the format versions that support each. Old files are not rewritten. Their statistics remain usable because readers can tell the original type from the encoded length. Narrowing is rejected since values could overflow, and changing a decimal’s scale would change what stored numbers mean. Even a widening can be refused for a column that feeds a partition field, if the new type would change partition values. Changing string to int is not allowed, because every old file would need rewriting and some values might not parse. For any such change, add a new column, backfill it, switch readers over and drop the old one. The example performs permitted promotions on a scratch table. From To Format versions int long 1, 2, 3 float double 1, 2, 3 decimal(P, S) decimal(P', S) with P’ greater than P 1, 2, 3 date timestamp, timestamp_ns (without time zone) 3 unknown any type 3 DROP TABLE IF EXISTS demo.shop.types PURGE; CREATE TABLE demo.shop.types (qty INT, price DECIMAL(10,2)) USING iceberg; ALTER TABLE demo.shop.types ALTER COLUMN qty TYPE BIGINT; ALTER TABLE demo.shop.types ALTER COLUMN price TYPE DECIMAL(14,2); 30. What is partition evolution? Partition evolution means changing the partition spec of an existing table. Each manifest records the spec its files were written with, so old data keeps its layout and new data uses the new one. ADD PARTITION FIELD, DROP PARTITION FIELD and REPLACE PARTITION FIELD change how future writes are partitioned, for instance from months to days. A query is projected onto each spec separately, so original fields prune old files and all fields prune new ones. You can evolve the spec again, and existing files keep whatever they had. This avoids rewriting a large table just to change its layout. Rewrite old files with rewrite_data_files only if queries on them need the new layout. Dynamic partition overwrite uses the current spec, so the same INSERT OVERWRITE can replace a different amount of data afterwards; check those jobs before making the change. Old and new layouts live side by side. ALTER TABLE demo.shop.orders ADD PARTITION FIELD bucket(4, customer_id); INSERT INTO demo.shop.orders (order_id, customer_id, amount, status, order_ts) VALUES (2001, 3, 15.00, 'NEW', TIMESTAMP '2026-11-02 08:00:00'); SELECT spec_id, count(*) AS files FROM demo.shop.orders.files GROUP BY spec_id; 31. Why does Iceberg not need to list directories? Iceberg does not need to list directories because its manifests already name every file in a snapshot. Planning reads metadata instead of asking storage what exists. A directory-based planner issues at least one listing for each partition, and object stores return listings in pages, so cost grows with partitions and files. Iceberg reads the manifest list and then only the manifests that might match. File statistics are already in those manifests, so footers need not be opened just to prune. It also helps correctness, since a listing cannot distinguish a finished file from one still being written or a leftover from a failed job, whereas a manifest lists only committed files. Listing does still happen in remove_orphan_files, which looks for files absent from metadata and is expensive for that reason. The thing to watch instead is too much metadata, visible in the manifests and files tables. 32. How do you choose a partitioning scheme? Choose a partitioning scheme from the filters your queries use and the amount of data per partition, and start coarse, because the spec can evolve later. Time-series tables usually use days(ts), or months(ts) when a day holds little data, and hours(ts) only at very high volume. A key used for point lookups or joins suits bucket(N, key), a column with few values that is always filtered can use identity, and a small table may need no partitioning. Estimate bytes per partition per day, and multiply cardinalities before combining fields. The common mistake is over-partitioning, which creates tiny files, heavy metadata and many open files per write, especially in streaming. For a second filter column, sorting often gives file skipping without multiplying partitions. Validate by running real queries, comparing files scanned with files in the table and checking the spread in the partitions table. 33. What is a table sort order, and how does it help? A table sort order is a declared ordering that writers apply, so each file covers a narrow range of the sort columns and its column bounds become selective. WRITE ORDERED BY range-shuffles data and orders it across tasks and within files. WRITE LOCALLY ORDERED BY sorts only within each file, and WRITE DISTRIBUTED BY PARTITION controls how rows are grouped without ordering them. These apply to new writes; existing files need a compaction with the sort strategy, and a Z-order rewrite can spread the benefit over several independent filter columns at some cost to the first. Without clustering, every file may span all values and a filter reads them all. Sorting adds work to each write, so it pays off when a table is read far more than it is written. It is also the better tool for high-cardinality columns, which would create huge numbers of tiny partitions. See sorting and clustering. Narrow ranges are what let a filter skip files. ALTER TABLE demo.shop.orders WRITE ORDERED BY customer_id, order_ts; unsorted file1 [cust 1..99] file2 [cust 0..98] -> filter reads both sorted file1 [cust 0..49] file2 [cust 50..99] -> filter reads one 34. What are the write distribution modes? The write distribution mode decides how rows are shuffled before files are written. The property write.distribution-mode accepts none, hash or range. With none there is no shuffle and each task writes whatever it holds, which is cheapest but can produce tasks times partitions files. hash shuffles by partition value, giving few files per partition. range samples the data and range-shuffles on partition and sort keys, producing globally ordered output at the highest cost. When the property is unset, Spark picks range for sorted tables, hash for partitioned ones and none otherwise. With 200 tasks each holding 30 days of data, none could write 6,000 files in one commit where hash writes about one per day. A very large partition under hash can be split by adaptive execution. Under none, rows must be clustered within tasks or the fanout writer enabled. Row-level operations have separate settings such as write.merge.distribution-mode. ALTER TABLE demo.shop.orders SET TBLPROPERTIES ( 'write.distribution-mode' = 'hash'); 35. What controls output file size? Output file size is controlled by write.target-file-size-bytes, 512 MB by default. It is a target rather than a guarantee. A task cannot write a file larger than the data it holds, files never cross partition boundaries, and compressed output is far smaller than the shuffle data it came from, while very large tasks roll over into several files. With a shuffling distribution mode, adaptive execution sizes write tasks from spark.sql.adaptive.advisoryPartitionSizeInBytes, which measures shuffle data and so usually has to exceed the file target. Large files suit full scans, while smaller ones can help selective queries and reduce copy-on-write rewrite cost. If files are far below target, for example 20 MB against 512 MB, each task or partition usually holds little data or commits are too frequent. Write reasonably sized files and let compaction reach the target. The statement below lowers it for one table. ALTER TABLE demo.shop.orders SET TBLPROPERTIES ( 'write.target-file-size-bytes' = '134217728'); 36. Why are small files a problem? Small files are a problem because each one adds a manifest entry, a request to open it and a footer to parse, whatever its size. Planning has more entries to read, scans spend their time opening files, compression works worse on little data, object stores charge and throttle by request, and merges have more files to join. The usual causes are frequent commits, fine partitioning, high write parallelism with little data and the none distribution mode. Measure by comparing average file size in the files table with the target and counting files per partition; no fixed size is too small, but files far below target in large numbers are the signal. Compaction repairs existing files, while longer triggers, coarser partitioning or hash distribution stop new ones. Storage is not freed until old snapshots expire, because they still reference the original files. 37. How does compaction work? Compaction in Iceberg is done by rewrite_data_files, which reads selected files and commits larger replacements in a replace snapshot. A file is a candidate when it is below 75% or above 180% of the target size, or when its deletes cross a threshold. Candidates are grouped per partition, and a group is rewritten if it has at least five files, holds more than one file totalling over the target size, exceeds the maximum file size or contains a file over a delete threshold. where limits the scope, strategy => 'sort' re-clusters data, rewrite-all ignores the selection rules, partial-progress.enabled commits group by group and max-concurrent-file-group-rewrites (default 5) sets parallelism. Delete rewriting is steered by delete-file-threshold, effectively off by default, and delete-ratio-threshold, 0.3. It is safe to run because results do not change. The commit fails if a rewritten file was removed or deleted from meanwhile, and the new files keep the starting sequence number so that later equality deletes still apply. If nothing is rewritten, no group met a trigger. CALL demo.system.rewrite_data_files( table => 'shop.orders', options => map('min-input-files', '2')); 38. What does expire_snapshots do? expire_snapshots removes old snapshots from metadata and deletes the files that no remaining snapshot references. It is what actually reclaims storage. Every branch and tag head is kept. On each branch, ancestors survive while they are younger than the age limit or within the minimum count, set by history.expire.max-snapshot-age-ms (five days) and history.expire.min-snapshots-to-keep (one). A run can override these with older_than and retain_last or name snapshot_ids. stream_results avoids collecting a huge delete list on the driver, max_concurrent_deletes deletes in parallel and clean_expired_metadata drops unused specs and schemas. Afterwards, time travel, rollback and incremental reads before the retained point no longer work. If nothing is deleted, the files are still held by a retained snapshot, often through a branch or tag, or the snapshots are too young. The date in the example is far in the future only so that everything on a test table qualifies. CALL demo.system.expire_snapshots( table => 'shop.orders', older_than => TIMESTAMP '2030-01-01 00:00:00', retain_last => 5); 39. What are orphan files, and how do you remove them? Orphan files are files under the table location that no metadata references, usually left behind by failed or killed jobs. remove_orphan_files finds and deletes them. The procedure lists the location, collects every file referenced by any snapshot’s metadata and treats the rest, beyond an age limit, as orphans. The limit defaults to three days and may not be under 24 hours, because a file from a write still in progress looks exactly like an orphan. Use dry_run to list without deleting and location to narrow the search. Expiry cannot do this job, since it never learns of files that no snapshot ever knew. Path forms are the main danger. If metadata stores one URI form and the listing returns another, live files appear unreferenced. equal_schemes and equal_authorities declare variants equivalent, and prefix_mismatch_mode defaults to ERROR; do not switch it to DELETE without understanding the mismatch. CALL demo.system.remove_orphan_files(table => 'shop.orders', dry_run => true); 40. When do you rewrite manifests? Rewrite manifests when planning is slow because the table has many small manifests, or manifests whose entries are spread across partitions so that none can be skipped. The procedure reads manifest entries, sorts and groups them by partition fields, writes reasonably sized manifests and commits a new snapshot. Data files are untouched. Iceberg already merges manifests during many commits when commit.manifest-merge.enabled is true, but streaming writes use fast appends by default, which skip merging, so streaming tables benefit most. The payoff is that a filter on one partition can then open only the manifests covering it. Check the count, size and partition summaries in the manifests table first, and compact small data files before this, since compaction changes the entries anyway. A rewrite invalidates cached plans for the table and can conflict with concurrent commits. CALL demo.system.rewrite_manifests('shop.orders'); before m1 [day1, day5, day9] m2 [day2, day5, day8] filter day5 reads both after m1 [day1, day2] m2 [day5] m3 [day8, day9] 41. Why do metadata files pile up, and how do you stop it? Metadata files pile up because every commit writes a new metadata.json and, by default, old ones are kept. Two table properties delete earlier files after each commit, with a default of 100 retained versions. That cleanup covers only files tracked in the metadata log, so any that left the log before it was enabled remain until orphan removal. The files also grow, since each lists every retained snapshot along with schemas and properties; expire_snapshots shrinks that list and removes the related manifest lists, while manifests are handled by rewrite_manifests, commit-time merging and expiry. This matters for tables that commit often. A table committing every minute without expiry rewrites an ever larger JSON file each time, which slows commits and raises the chance of conflicts. On an old table, check the file size and snapshot count, expire snapshots first, then enable the cleanup shown below. ALTER TABLE demo.shop.orders SET TBLPROPERTIES ( 'write.metadata.delete-after-commit.enabled' = 'true', 'write.metadata.previous-versions-max' = '50'); 42. What is the difference between a branch and a tag? Branches and tags are both named references to a snapshot. A branch moves as you commit to it, while a tag stays on one snapshot. A branch accepts writes and suits audits, experiments and backfills; a tag marks releases or month-end states. Either one protects its snapshot from expiry. RETAIN sets a maximum reference age, measured from the snapshot’s age, after which expiry may drop the reference; main is never dropped. Branches can also keep a number of snapshots. Write to a branch with table.branch_<name>, or set spark.wap.branch, which works only when the table has write.wap.enabled=true and otherwise silently writes to main. References share data files with main, so creating one is cheap, but a long-lived one keeps old files alive and costs storage. The schema belongs to the whole table. To publish a branch, use fast_forward if main has not moved, or cherry-pick; there is no three-way merge. A branch is a second line of history. ALTER TABLE demo.shop.orders CREATE BRANCH etl_test RETAIN 7 DAYS; ALTER TABLE demo.shop.orders CREATE TAG month_end RETAIN 365 DAYS; 43. What is write-audit-publish? Write-audit-publish means writing data where consumers cannot see it, validating it, and then publishing it with one metadata operation. With branches, a job commits to a named branch, checks run against it, and fast_forward moves main, which succeeds only if main has not diverged. The other method sets write.wap.enabled and a session spark.wap.id, which stages an unreferenced snapshot that publish_changes later applies as a new one; it fails if the ID was used for several snapshots. Good audits check counts against the source, nulls and ranges, duplicate keys and business totals. Consumers therefore never see a batch that failed its checks. If main moves during an audit, recreate the branch from the new head or cherry-pick the audited commit. Give audit branches a retention period so failed runs do not hold files forever, and remember that a branch is not access control. ALTER TABLE demo.shop.orders CREATE BRANCH audit; INSERT INTO demo.shop.orders.branch_audit (order_id, customer_id, amount, status, order_ts) VALUES (5001, 1, 10.00, 'NEW', TIMESTAMP '2026-11-03 09:00:00'); SELECT count(*) FROM demo.shop.orders.branch_audit WHERE amount < 0; CALL demo.system.fast_forward('shop.orders', 'main', 'audit'); 44. How do you read only the data added between two snapshots? To read only new data, use an incremental read with start-snapshot-id, which is exclusive, and end-snapshot-id, which is inclusive. It returns the rows added by append commits in that range. Iceberg walks the snapshots between the two IDs and reads the files those appends added, without comparing table states, so it is cheap. Both snapshots must still exist on the same line of history. Updates, deletes and overwrites in the range are not represented, so tables changed in place need the changelog view instead. A pipeline stores the last processed snapshot ID with its output, reads from there to the current snapshot and saves both together or in a way that is safe to repeat. If expiry removes the stored ID, the job cannot resume and needs a full reload, so keep snapshots longer than the longest outage you expect. ids = [r.snapshot_id for r in spark.sql( "SELECT snapshot_id FROM demo.shop.orders.snapshots " "WHERE operation = 'append' ORDER BY committed_at").collect()] start_id, end_id = ids[-2], ids[-1] (spark.read.format("iceberg") .option("start-snapshot-id", start_id) .option("end-snapshot-id", end_id) .load("demo.shop.orders")) 45. How do you capture row-level changes from an Iceberg table? Row-level changes come from a changelog view over a snapshot range. It reports inserted and deleted rows with the columns _change_type, _change_ordinal and _commit_snapshot_id. Iceberg records files and deleted positions, not logical updates, so an update looks like a delete plus an insert. Passing identifier_columns pairs them, compute_updates produces before and after images, and net_changes collapses intermediate changes to their net effect; the last two cannot be combined. The options argument sets the snapshot or timestamp range. Removing rows that were merely carried over by a copy-on-write rewrite costs extra work on large rewrites. This gives downstream jobs the changes to a table that is updated in place. It is limited to retained snapshots, some delete types are not supported, and it shows differences between commits rather than every source event, so it does not replace change capture at the database. CALL demo.system.create_changelog_view(table => 'shop.orders', changelog_view => 'orders_changes'); SELECT _change_type, count(*) FROM orders_changes GROUP BY _change_type; 46. Why does a MERGE fail with MERGE_CARDINALITY_VIOLATION? MERGE_CARDINALITY_VIOLATION means more than one source row matched the same target row, so the result would be ambiguous. The fix is to deduplicate the source, keeping one row per key ordered by a sequence that comes from the source system. Arrival time is a poor choice, because retries and out-of-order delivery would let an older version win. Two source rows with a key that does not yet exist raise no error and are both inserted. Two related traps pass silently. If the match condition is not unique in the target, every matching target row is updated, and without a guard such as `s.seq t.seq` a replayed batch can overwrite newer data. Identifier fields declare which columns identify a row, but writes are not checked against them, so the pipeline must enforce and monitor uniqueness itself. target: key=1 source: key=1 'b', key=1 'c' -> error target: no key=2 source: key=2 'b', key=2 'c' -> both inserted SELECT order_id, status FROM ( SELECT *, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY order_ts DESC) AS rn FROM demo.shop.orders ) latest WHERE rn = 1 LIMIT 5; 47. What are position deletes and equality deletes? A position delete names a data file and a row position. An equality delete names column values, such as an ID, without knowing where the row is. To write a position delete, the writer must read the target to find the row, and readers then simply skip known positions in one file. An equality delete needs no lookup, which is why streaming upsert writers such as Flink use it: they write “delete key 42” and the new row, leaving the matching to readers. Those deletes apply to older files in the partition, or to all files if global. In format version 3, new position deletes are written as deletion vectors. The cost lands on queries, which must load equality delete values and check them against every applicable file, often as an in-memory join. Compact data files so that deletes are applied and removed, frequently for equality deletes. The query below counts files by content: 0 data, 1 position deletes, 2 equality deletes. SELECT content, count(*) FROM demo.shop.orders.files GROUP BY content; 48. What is the difference between static and dynamic partition overwrite? The two modes decide what INSERT OVERWRITE replaces. In static mode, Spark’s default, it replaces the whole table unless a partition is given; in dynamic mode it replaces only the partitions that receive rows. Iceberg recommends dynamic mode, or MERGE INTO. The DataFrame v2 writer makes the choice explicit: writeTo(t).overwritePartitions() is dynamic, while writeTo(t).overwrite(condition) replaces rows matching a filter. With hidden partitioning, which partitions count as touched depends on the current spec, so after evolution a job that replaced a day might replace a bucket of a day or a whole month. The difference is dangerous with an empty source, where static mode can empty the table. For a safe backfill, overwrite with an explicit condition, run it on a branch, validate the result and publish it. SET spark.sql.sources.partitionOverwriteMode=dynamic; INSERT OVERWRITE demo.shop.orders (order_id, customer_id, amount, status, order_ts) VALUES (6001, 2, 20.00, 'NEW', TIMESTAMP '2026-11-04 10:00:00'); SET spark.sql.sources.partitionOverwriteMode=static; 49. How do you choose a catalog? Choose a catalog from the engines that must connect, how access is controlled, the commit rate and what you already operate. A REST catalog suits many engines and central security, at the price of running or buying the server. Hive Metastore suits existing Hadoop platforms and commits by checking and swapping the table entry; AWS Glue suits AWS platforms through conditional updates. JDBC uses a database row and works for small deployments, though every client needs database access. Nessie adds branching across tables, and the Hadoop catalog belongs only in local tests. Before deciding, confirm that every engine supports it, find out who authorises access and issues storage credentials, check the sustained commit rate and plan for outages and restores. Tables can move by registering their metadata elsewhere, but permissions, views and automation move with more effort, so the choice tends to stick. See Iceberg catalogs. 50. Why is the Hadoop catalog unsafe on object storage? The Hadoop catalog commits by renaming a file to the next version number, and it depends on that rename being atomic and failing if the target already exists. Many object stores give no such guarantee, because a rename is often a copy followed by a delete. Two writers can then both appear to succeed while one commit is lost. Nothing fails at write time; later you find missing rows, snapshots gone from history or a stale version-hint.text. The specification marks this file-system table scheme as deprecated and calls it unsafe in object stores and local file systems. It is acceptable for local development, tests and single-writer experiments such as the examples here. Anywhere else, use a catalog with a real compare-and-swap and register the existing metadata file in it. A lock manager helps only if every client cooperates. writer A: write tmp-a.json -> rename to v8.metadata.json writer B: write tmp-b.json -> rename to v8.metadata.json HDFS: second rename fails, B retries some stores: second rename may overwrite, A's commit is lost 51. What are Iceberg views? An Iceberg view is a view definition stored under its own specification, so that engines can share it. It keeps the SQL text with its dialect, the output columns and types, a history of versions with one marked current, and the default catalog and namespace used to resolve names. A view created by one engine is visible to others through the catalog, and replacing it is an atomic, versioned change. It stores no data and materialises nothing. Sharing is not translation, though. An engine needs a representation in a dialect it understands, so SQL with engine-specific functions or casts may not run elsewhere. Prefer standard SQL and test each view in every engine that uses it. Support depends on the catalog; the Hadoop catalog has none, which is why there is no runnable example here. See Iceberg views. 52. How do you migrate a Hive table to Iceberg? A Hive table can be migrated with the snapshot, migrate or add_files procedures, or by rewriting its data into a new Iceberg table. snapshot creates an Iceberg table over the source files and leaves the source unchanged, which makes it ideal for rehearsal, although that table does not own the files, has expiry disabled and can break if the source changes. migrate replaces the table in place, renaming the original to a backup by default; it needs Parquet, ORC or Avro and refuses bucketed tables. add_files imports files into an existing table without checking their schema, and expiry may later delete them; it refuses already referenced files by default, but with check_duplicate_files => false adding one twice duplicates its rows. In-place methods read footers, record statistics and add a name mapping without copying data. Rewrite when partitioning or file sizes are poor, and migrate in place when the layout is already good. To roll back, stop writers, drop the new table without purging and restore the backup, which lacks later writes. See Hive to Iceberg migration. Rehearse with snapshot, cut over with migrate. 53. What does register_table do? register_table adds an existing Iceberg table to a catalog by pointing at one of its metadata files. No data is copied. It is used to move a table between catalogs, to recreate an entry after a drop that kept the files, and to bring up a replicated copy during disaster recovery. For a move, stop writers, note the final metadata location, register it, repoint clients, verify and then remove the old entry without purging. If storage has moved, prepare the absolute paths with rewrite_table_path and copy the files first. Two mistakes lose data. Registering an older metadata file silently drops every later commit, and later maintenance may delete files the newer history needs. Leaving the table writable in two catalogs makes their pointers diverge, and cleanup in one can remove files the other still references. CALL <catalog>.system.register_table( table => 'db.orders', metadata_file => 's3://bucket/warehouse/db/orders/metadata/00042-<uuid>.metadata.json'); 54. How does Spark Structured Streaming write to Iceberg? Spark Structured Streaming commits each micro-batch to an Iceberg table as one snapshot, in append or complete output mode. For exactly-once delivery, the sink records the query ID and epoch ID in the snapshot summary. Before committing, it walks back through the current history for this query’s last epoch and skips a batch already present. Appends are fast appends unless use-merge-append-for-streaming is set, and fanout-enabled keeps a writer open per partition to avoid sorting. The trigger interval decides commit frequency; Iceberg recommends at least a minute, and longer triggers give fewer, larger files. Compaction and expiry are still needed. The guarantee covers this sink and its checkpoint only: a new checkpoint means a new query ID, foreachBatch writes must be made idempotent yourself, and aggressive expiry can remove the snapshots the check relies on. Remove the checkpoint before resetting the table and rerunning the example. One micro-batch, one commit. events = (spark.readStream.format("rate").option("rowsPerSecond", 5).load() .selectExpr("value AS order_id", "value AS customer_id", "CAST(1 AS DECIMAL(12,2)) AS amount", "'NEW' AS status", "timestamp AS order_ts")) query = (events.writeStream.format("iceberg") .outputMode("append") .trigger(processingTime="1 minute") .option("checkpointLocation", "/tmp/ckpt/orders") .toTable("demo.shop.orders")) # after a few triggers: query.stop() 55. Can you stream from an Iceberg table? Yes. Spark can read an Iceberg table as a stream, picking up newly appended files incrementally and keeping its position in the checkpoint. Each micro-batch plans the files added since the recorded snapshot and file. stream-from-timestamp chooses where to start, and streaming-max-files-per-micro-batch or streaming-max-rows-per-micro-batch limit batch size, which stops catch-up after downtime from becoming one enormous batch. The source is designed for appends. An overwrite or delete snapshot stops the query unless you set streaming-skip-overwrite-snapshots or streaming-skip-delete-snapshots, and skipping means the change never reaches downstream. Compaction commits add no new rows and are not replayed. For tables with updates, run the changelog view in a batch loop or stream from an append-only raw table, and keep snapshot expiry behind the slowest consumer. 56. How do you upgrade the format version? You upgrade a table by setting its format-version property. The change touches metadata only. Going from version 1 to 2 introduces sequence numbers and allows row-level deletes. Going from 2 to 3 makes new deletes use deletion vectors and starts row lineage for new snapshots. Existing files are not rewritten, and old position delete files remain valid until that file’s deletes are written again. There is no downgrade, only copying into a new table at the lower version, which loses history. So list every reader, writer and maintenance job first, confirm each supports both the version and the features you will start using, rehearse on a test table with the same properties, upgrade readers before writers and have a recovery plan. DROP TABLE IF EXISTS demo.shop.upgrade_demo PURGE; CREATE TABLE demo.shop.upgrade_demo (id BIGINT) USING iceberg; ALTER TABLE demo.shop.upgrade_demo SET TBLPROPERTIES ('format-version' = '3'); 57. What does write.object-storage.enabled do? write.object-storage.enabled adds a hash-based prefix to data file paths so that requests spread across many object-store key prefixes. It is off by default. Object stores scale request rates by key range, so a table whose newest files all share one date prefix concentrates traffic and can be throttled. The hash comes from the file name, combined with the partition path on partitioned tables when write.object-storage.partitioned-paths includes it. Iceberg reads are unaffected, because paths come from metadata. The trade-off is that directories become hard to browse and anything assuming a partition layout, such as lifecycle rules or scripts, stops working. Existing files keep their paths until rewritten. Small tables, low concurrency and file systems such as HDFS do not need it. default .../data/order_ts_day=2026-11-01/00000-....parquet enabled .../data/<hash dirs>/order_ts_day=2026-11-01/00000-....parquet 58. Which table properties do you review first on a production table? On a production table, review the format version, file size and distribution mode, row-level write modes, column metrics, snapshot retention, metadata cleanup and commit retries first. Those settings decide who can read the table, how files are laid out, what queries can skip, how far back you can recover and how writers cope with contention. The table below lists each property with its default and the question to ask. SHOW TBLPROPERTIES displays only what has been set; anything absent uses the library default, which can differ between versions. Set them early, because layout properties affect only data written afterwards. Treat retention as a recovery decision as much as a cost one. Property Default Question to ask format-version 2 Do all engines support it? write.target-file-size-bytes 536870912 Does it match the query pattern? write.distribution-mode unset Is the chosen shuffle producing sensible files? write.delete.mode, write.update.mode, write.merge.mode copy-on-write How often do rows change? write.metadata.metrics.default truncate(16) Are filter columns covered? history.expire.max-snapshot-age-ms 5 days How far back must you recover? history.expire.min-snapshots-to-keep 1 Minimum history for idle tables? write.metadata.delete-after-commit.enabled false Will metadata files pile up? commit.retry.num-retries 4 How many writers compete? SHOW TBLPROPERTIES demo.shop.orders; 59. What Spark configuration does Iceberg need? Spark needs three things for Iceberg: the runtime jar, a catalog declared under spark.sql.catalog.<name> and the Iceberg SQL extensions. The artifact name carries the Spark and Scala versions, and a mismatch typically fails with NoSuchMethodError or a missing class; cloud storage may need an extra SDK bundle. SparkCatalog adds a separate Iceberg catalog, while SparkSessionCatalog wraps the built-in spark_catalog so Iceberg and other tables share names, which migration procedures rely on. One session can declare several catalogs and qualify table names with them. Extensions are read when the session is built, and on Spark Connect they belong on the server. A misspelt extension class only logs a warning, so the first symptom may be a PARSE_SYNTAX_ERROR on an ALTER TABLE. The main settings are listed below. Setting Purpose --packages org.apache.iceberg:iceberg-spark-runtime-<spark>_<scala>:<version> The integration jar spark.sql.catalog.<name> Catalog implementation class spark.sql.catalog.<name>.type and .uri, .warehouse Which catalog and where spark.sql.extensions org.apache.iceberg.spark.extensions.IcebergSparkSessionExtensions 60. How do you check the health of a table? You check a table’s health by querying its metadata tables for file sizes, delete files, manifests and snapshots, and watching how they change. Falling average file size calls for compaction and better writers. Growing delete files or records call for compaction with delete thresholds, many manifests with slow planning call for a manifest rewrite, a very old and long snapshot list calls for expiry and a look at references, and one outsized partition points to skew. In the query below, content 0 means data, 1 position deletes and 2 equality deletes. A single reading says little, so run the checks on a schedule, store the results and alert on trends. Add evidence from the query side as well, such as planning time, files scanned and commit failures, which shows whether the layout is actually hurting. SELECT content, count(*) AS files, round(avg(file_size_in_bytes) / 1048576, 2) AS avg_mb, sum(record_count) AS records FROM demo.shop.orders.files GROUP BY content; SELECT count(*) AS manifests, sum(length) AS manifest_bytes FROM demo.shop.orders.manifests; SELECT count(*) AS snapshots, min(committed_at) AS oldest FROM demo.shop.orders.snapshots; Advanced 61. Walk through the commit protocol. In the commit protocol, a writer builds new files and metadata from the current table version, then asks the catalog to switch the pointer only if that version is still current. It reads the current metadata as its base, writes data and delete files, then manifests, a manifest list and a new metadata file, and requests the swap. If another writer got there first, it reloads, checks that its change is still valid and retries. An append requires nothing. A compaction requires its replaced files to be present with no new position deletes, a file delete requires its files, row-level changes require no conflicting data or deletes at their isolation level, and schema or spec changes require the old definition to be unchanged. No locks are held during the work, which favours workloads with rare conflicts. Retries reuse data files and often manifests, and the whole design rests on the catalog’s compare-and-swap. A commit is new files plus one conditional pointer swap. 62. Compare CommitFailedException, ValidationException and CommitStateUnknownException. The three exceptions mean that a commit lost a race, that it is no longer valid against newer changes, or that nobody knows whether it happened. CommitFailedException comes from the catalog rejecting the swap; it is safe to retry, and Iceberg retries automatically first. ValidationException comes from checking the new base during a retry, for example “Found conflicting files that can contain records matching” the operation’s filter, so the whole operation must be recomputed or the overlap removed. CommitStateUnknownException arises when the request was sent and no definite answer returned, such as after a network timeout. The third is the dangerous one. If the commit succeeded, its files are live, so deleting them would corrupt the table and rerunning could apply the change twice. Check the table before acting. Jobs become safe to repeat by merging on a business key, overwriting a deterministic partition or recording a batch ID in the snapshot summary. CommitFailedException let retries run; if exhausted, reduce contention ValidationException recompute from the new table state CommitStateUnknownException query snapshots; decide; then rerun if absent 63. What isolation levels do row-level operations offer? Row-level operations offer serializable, the default, and snapshot isolation, set per command with write.delete.isolation-level, write.update.isolation-level and write.merge.isolation-level. Under both, a commit fails if another removed or rewrote a file it depends on, or added deletes for rows being updated, and changes outside the operation’s filter are allowed. They differ on new data: serializable rejects a concurrent append that matches the filter, while snapshot isolation permits it. So an UPDATE ... WHERE status = 'NEW' can commit under snapshot isolation while newly appended NEW rows stay unchanged, a result no serial order would produce. Readers always see one committed snapshot either way. Keep serializable unless the pipeline can tolerate rows appearing concurrently, such as heavy ingestion beside corrections to older data. A filter on the partition column avoids most false conflicts. ALTER TABLE demo.shop.orders SET TBLPROPERTIES ( 'write.delete.isolation-level' = 'serializable', 'write.merge.isolation-level' = 'serializable'); 64. How are commit retries configured? Four table properties control how a writer retries a lost commit: commit.retry.num-retries (default 4), commit.retry.min-wait-ms (100), commit.retry.max-wait-ms (60,000) and commit.retry.total-timeout-ms (1,800,000). After a rejected swap, the writer waits with exponential back-off between the minimum and maximum, refreshes the table, revalidates and tries again until attempts or time run out. This resolves contention among compatible operations, mainly appends. It cannot resolve validation failures, which are logical conflicts, or a commit rate higher than the catalog and metadata size allow. Tune by first reducing commit frequency and competing writers, then keeping metadata small so each attempt is short, and only then raising retries, as the example does. Very high counts hide a design problem and lengthen job tails. Rising attempts per commit in reports and driver logs are an early warning. ALTER TABLE demo.shop.orders SET TBLPROPERTIES ( 'commit.retry.num-retries' = '10'); 65. What are sequence numbers for? Sequence numbers give commits a reliable order. Each successful commit receives an increasing number, and files carry the number of the commit that added them, which tells Iceberg which delete files apply to which data files. Each file has a data sequence number, stating how old its data is logically and used to match deletes, and a file sequence number, recording when it was added. They differ after compaction, which writes new files that keep the older data number; otherwise an equality delete committed during the rewrite would stop applying and deleted rows would return. The manifest list also records each manifest’s min_sequence_number, which helps planning discard deletes that can no longer apply. Clocks on different writers could not provide this order. New manifest entries store null and inherit the number at commit, so a retried commit gets a new one without rewriting manifests, and files in tables upgraded from version 1 count as 0. seq 1 data file A seq 2 equality delete "id = 7" applies to A (1 < 2) data file B added in seq 2 not affected (2 is not < 2) seq 3 data file C with id = 7 not affected 66. When does a delete file apply to a data file? A delete file applies to a data file when the data is old enough and in scope. A deletion vector or position delete applies when the data file’s sequence number is at most the delete’s, the partition spec and values match and the file is referenced; position deletes are ignored for a file that has a deletion vector, since the vector must already include them. An equality delete requires a strictly older data file in the same partition, unless it was written unpartitioned, in which case it applies everywhere, which is powerful and expensive. The two rules differ for a reason. “At most” lets one commit add a file and delete positions in it, as streaming writers must, while “strictly less” lets one commit delete a key and insert its new version safely. After partition evolution, an old partition-scoped delete does not reach new files. A file with many applicable deletes costs more to scan. 67. What are deletion vectors, and why replace position delete files? A deletion vector is a bitmap of deleted row positions for one data file, stored as a blob in a Puffin file. It was introduced in format version 3 to replace position delete files. Positions are kept in Roaring bitmaps, compact for both sparse and dense deletions, and one Puffin file can hold vectors for many data files. The manifest records the file, offset and length, and there is at most one vector per data file in a snapshot. A new delete merges with the existing vector and replaces it, so concurrent deletes to the same file conflict. Old position delete files stay valid after an upgrade until that file’s deletes are next written. Readers benefit by loading one bitmap and testing positions instead of finding and merging many delete files. Deleted rows are still stored and read before being skipped, so rewrite heavily deleted files. The example uses the version 3 table from question 56. Position delete file on the left, deletion vector on the right. INSERT INTO demo.shop.upgrade_demo SELECT /*+ COALESCE(1) */ id FROM range(10); ALTER TABLE demo.shop.upgrade_demo SET TBLPROPERTIES ('write.delete.mode' = 'merge-on-read'); DELETE FROM demo.shop.upgrade_demo WHERE id = 3; SELECT file_format, record_count FROM demo.shop.upgrade_demo.delete_files; 68. What is row lineage? Row lineage, added in format version 3, gives every row a stable ID and records which commit last changed it, exposed as _row_id and _last_updated_sequence_number. IDs are inherited: a data file receives a first row ID, and each row’s ID is that value plus its position, while the table tracks the next unused number. New rows need nothing written, which keeps commit retries cheap. When compaction or copy-on-write moves a row, its ID is copied; a modified row leaves the last-updated value empty so it takes the new commit’s number. This lets incremental processing distinguish a changed row from a new one and supports auditing. Rows changed through equality deletes lose their identity, because the writer never read the old row, and snapshots from before an upgrade have no IDs. A row ID also says nothing about business uniqueness. 69. What else does format version 3 add, and what is the status of version 4? Format version 3 adds, besides deletion vectors and row lineage, new types, default values, multi-argument transforms and table encryption keys. Version 4 is still being designed. The new types are variant for semi-structured data, geometry and geography for spatial data, nanosecond timestamps and unknown for a column whose type is not yet decided. An initial-default fills a new column for older rows, and a write-default applies to later writes that omit it. Version 4 is not formally adopted, its documented change so far is relative paths in metadata, and it should not be used in production. A feature in the specification is usable only when every engine on the table implements it for reading and writing; variant, for instance, needs an engine with that type. Verify each engine, trial on a new table and then upgrade. 70. How does a REST catalog change commits and security? With a REST catalog, the client sends requirements and updates, and the server applies the updates only if every requirement still holds. Requirements include assert-table-uuid against a replaced table, assert-ref-snapshot-id against a moved branch, schema and partition spec checks against concurrent changes and assert-create for new tables. The server writes the metadata file and swaps the pointer. It can authorise each operation and issue short-lived storage credentials or sign requests, so engines need no long-lived keys. The specification also defines multi-table commits and server-side planning, which servers may or may not implement. Compared with clients swapping a pointer, conflict checks are finer, commit logic lives in one place for every language and policy can be enforced centrally. The cost is that the service’s availability, latency, backups and authentication become critical. Apache Polaris is one implementation. One REST catalog implementation handling a request. 71. What is the difference between a fast append and a merge append? A fast append writes a new manifest for the new files and reuses the others. A merge append may also combine small manifests during the commit. Fast append does minimal work and keeps the conflict window short, but manifests accumulate and planning degrades without maintenance. Merge append reads and rewrites some manifests, which keeps their number in check at the cost of a longer commit. Merging begins at commit.manifest.min-count-to-merge (100), targets commit.manifest.target-size-bytes (8 MB) and can be disabled with commit.manifest-merge.enabled. Spark batch appends merge, while Structured Streaming uses fast appends unless use-merge-append-for-streaming is set. So a streaming table can collect thousands of manifests. Count them with the query below, then rewrite them on a schedule or accept slightly slower commits by merging. SELECT count(*) AS manifests, avg(length) AS avg_bytes FROM demo.shop.orders.manifests; 72. How are files turned into Spark tasks? Spark tasks are built by splitting large Iceberg files and packing small ones together. Large files are divided at row group boundaries, and pieces are combined until a task reaches read.split.target-size, 128 MB by default. Every file counts at least read.split.open-file-cost, 4 MB, so a task does not receive thousands of tiny files, and read.split.planning-lookback, 10, sets how many bins stay open while packing. Spark may adjust split size to the scan and available parallelism, and the split-size read option overrides it for one query. Task counts therefore reflect file layout. Many very short tasks suggest a small split size or tiny files, while a few long tasks on a large cluster suggest the opposite or unsplittable input. Tasks must also apply deletes, which byte sizes do not show. target 128 MB, open cost 4 MB file of 20 KB counts as 4 MB -> at most about 32 tiny files per task 73. What is a storage-partitioned join? A storage-partitioned join lets Spark join two tables partition by partition, with no shuffle, when both are partitioned compatibly on the join keys. It needs spark.sql.sources.v2.bucketing.enabled and the Iceberg setting spark.sql.iceberg.planning.preserve-data-grouping, matching transforms on the join columns, and a join condition that covers them. Further Spark settings handle partition values present on only one side and ease skew by partially clustering one side. Parallelism is limited by the number of partitions, so a skewed partition becomes a skewed task. It pays off when both tables are large and joined repeatedly on the same key; if one side is small, a broadcast join is simpler. Confirm that it happened by looking for the absence of Exchange under both sides in the physical plan. The two settings are shown below. orders bucket(16, customer_id) customers bucket(16, id) bucket 0 <-------- join in one task --------> bucket 0 bucket 1 <-------- join in one task --------> bucket 1 SET spark.sql.sources.v2.bucketing.enabled = true; SET `spark.sql.iceberg.planning.preserve-data-grouping` = true; 74. How do you run compaction alongside active writers? Run compaction alongside writers by limiting it to data that is not changing and letting it commit in pieces, so that a conflict loses little. Appends never conflict with compaction. A copy-on-write update of a file being compacted, or new position deletes against it, does conflict, while new equality deletes still apply afterwards thanks to the preserved sequence number. Filter with where to partitions no longer receiving changes, enable partial-progress.enabled so that groups commit separately, keep file groups small and schedule around heavy merge jobs. Partial progress means more snapshots and a result that may be only partly applied, with failed groups logged. A finished job does not prove the table was compacted, so compare files before and after and read the output. When one side has to lose, let it be compaction, which can be repeated without hurting freshness. 75. Why can delete files survive a compaction? Delete files can survive a data compaction because it replaces data files and may leave delete files pointing at files that are no longer live. These dangling deletes change no result but still cost planning and storage. rewrite_data_files applies deletes into new files when delete-file-threshold or delete-ratio-threshold selects them, and with remove-dangling-deletes it also drops the ones that no longer apply. rewrite_position_delete_files compacts position delete files and removes dangling positions. By default a file is not rewritten for deletes until they reach 30% of its rows, and the position delete procedure may select nothing. So check counts after running them. Removal based on sequence numbers misses some cases, such as global equality deletes that match nothing, behaviour has changed between releases, and storage stays used until old snapshots expire. See copy-on-write or merge-on-read. How a delete file can outlive the data it applied to. 76. What are Puffin files and table statistics? Puffin is a file format for blobs that do not fit in manifests, a container whose footer describes each blob’s type, fields, snapshot and offset. Iceberg uses it for deletion vectors and for table statistics. The statistics are distinct-value estimates per column, stored as Apache DataSketches theta sketches and computed by compute_table_stats, which covers all top-level primitive columns unless the columns argument narrows it. Partition statistics are a separate file with per-partition counts, produced by compute_partition_stats. Cost-based optimisers need distinct counts to estimate join sizes and choose join order and build side, which column bounds cannot provide. The sketches belong to one snapshot and do not refresh themselves, so recompute them after large changes. They help only if the engine reads them, so compare plans before and after. CALL demo.system.compute_table_stats('shop.orders'); 77. Why might one session not see another session's commit? A session may not see another session’s commit because its catalog is serving a cached copy of the table. Caching is on by default (spark.sql.catalog.<name>.cache-enabled) with an expiry of 30,000 milliseconds. The timer restarts on every access, so a session that queries more often than every 30 seconds can keep reading an earlier snapshot indefinitely. The cache avoids repeated catalog calls and metadata reads and keeps references within a query consistent. To see the new data, run REFRESH TABLE, disable the cache or shorten the expiry, accepting more catalog traffic; a value of -1 turns expiry off entirely. The same symptom can come from a branch or time-travel setting in the session, two catalogs pointing at different metadata or a commit that failed, so compare the session’s snapshot ID with the writer’s. REFRESH TABLE demo.shop.orders; 78. Does Iceberg support multi-table transactions? Not through the table format itself, which commits one table at a time. Some support exists around it. The REST specification has a multi-table commit endpoint, though server and engine support vary, and a catalog such as Nessie can publish many tables by merging a branch, provided everyone uses that catalog. Without these, you can write every table to a branch, validate and fast-forward them one after another, tag all tables with the same batch name after loading, or make jobs idempotent so a rerun repairs a partial failure. This matters when readers must see related tables agree. They then need to read a published set, by tag or recorded snapshot ID, instead of each table’s latest state. If a two-table job fails halfway, finish it by rerunning, or roll back the first table if nobody has committed to it since. 79. How do you honour a right-to-erasure request? To honour a right-to-erasure request, delete the rows, rewrite the files that held them, remove the references and snapshots that keep old versions, and clean up storage. A DELETE only changes the current snapshot, and with merge-on-read the original data file still contains the row until compaction. Forgotten tags and branches keep everything they reference, old metadata can hold identifiers in column statistics and partition values until it expires, and raw tables, derived tables, exports, object versions and backups need the same treatment. Verify the removal across all snapshots, not just the current one. It is far easier when designed in: keep personal data in few tables, cluster by the subject key so deletes rewrite little, set retention shorter than the legal deadline and record evidence. Per-subject encryption keys that can be destroyed are an alternative. DELETE current snapshot no longer shows the rows compaction data files rewritten without them (needed for merge-on-read) drop refs branches and tags stop protecting old snapshots expire old snapshots removed, their files deleted orphan cleanup leftovers from failed jobs removed storage object versions, backups and replicas handled 80. What do you check before several engines write to one table? Before several engines write to one table, confirm that they share a catalog, support the same format features and agree on who maintains it. Two catalogs would lose commits. One engine lagging on format version or delete types can break reads or return wrong rows. Time zone and timestamp handling differ, some writers ignore partition or sort hints, and each has its own retry defaults. Table properties are shared but not always honoured, so verify behaviour rather than settings. Assign one owner for maintenance and keep retention longer than the slowest consumer needs. Prefer one writer per table or partition range, since a streaming upsert and a batch merge on the same partitions will keep failing validation. Test each engine’s writes, updates, deletes and reads, run the engines concurrently, compare results on a pinned snapshot and repeat on upgrades. Block old writers in the catalog before enabling new features. Scenario-based Each question starts from a symptom. Say what you would look at first, why, and what you would change. 81. Queries have slowed steadily over three weeks with no data growth. What do you do? When queries slow down steadily without data growth, first find whether the time goes into planning or execution, then use metadata tables to see what changed. A long gap before tasks start points to too many manifests or snapshots; many short tasks to small files; slow tasks on a changing table to delete build-up; reading far more files than expected to overlapping bounds; and one slow task to skew. Their fixes are manifest rewriting and expiry, compaction, delete compaction, sorting, and addressing the skew. The query below shows which partitions hold the most files. Since volume is unchanged, look for more frequent commits, a new writer, a disabled maintenance job or a new query pattern, using snapshot summaries over time. Compaction repairs today’s state and a schedule stops a repeat. If it changes nothing, check that it selected files and did not fail. SELECT partition, file_count, record_count FROM demo.shop.orders.partitions ORDER BY file_count DESC LIMIT 10; 82. Storage keeps growing although the row count is flat. Why? Storage grows with a flat row count because old snapshots keep old files alive. Every compaction, update or overwrite adds new files while earlier snapshots still reference the previous ones. Check the oldest snapshot and the snapshot count to see whether expiry is succeeding, then look in refs for a forgotten branch or tag. Compare live bytes with all bytes reachable from any snapshot, using the query below, dry run orphan removal for failed jobs, and consider object versioning, incomplete multipart uploads and backups. Metadata files add to the total on frequently committed tables. A large gap between reachable and live data means history is the cost, so shorten retention or drop references, agreeing it with data owners because retention is how far back mistakes can be undone. If reachable data is small but the bucket is large, look for orphan files or old object versions. -- both include data files and delete files SELECT sum(file_size_in_bytes) AS live_bytes FROM demo.shop.orders.files; SELECT sum(file_size_in_bytes) AS reachable_bytes FROM ( SELECT DISTINCT file_path, file_size_in_bytes FROM demo.shop.orders.all_files ) f; 83. Twenty jobs append to one table and some fail with CommitFailedException. How do you fix it? Twenty appending jobs fail with CommitFailedException because they lose the pointer swap more times than their retry budget allows. Appends never conflict logically, so this is pure contention. Confirm the exception is not ValidationException, then measure commits per minute and commit duration. The chance of collision rises with both, since the window between reading the base and swapping the pointer is where others get in, and a bloated metadata file widens it. Make fewer commits through longer triggers or fewer writers, then shorten each commit by expiring snapshots, rewriting manifests and checking catalog capacity, and only then raise the retry settings, which lengthens job tails. If the design allows, have producers write to a queue that a single job commits, or give independent sources their own tables, combined later by a view or merge. chance of a collision rises with: commit rate x commit duration 84. Two MERGE jobs fail intermittently with ValidationException. What is happening? Two merge jobs fail with ValidationException when each finds that the other changed files or added rows covered by its own condition. Retrying the commit cannot fix a logical conflict. The message names the conflicting files. Typically both jobs match on the key only, so each conflict filter covers the whole table even though their data does not overlap. Adding a literal partition predicate to the ON clause, such as t.region = 'EU', lets Iceberg see that they are disjoint. Otherwise give each job its own partitions, run overlapping jobs one after another or combine them, and keep them short. Snapshot isolation helps only where ignoring concurrent appends is safe, and never lets two writers rewrite the same files. A rerun must execute the whole merge against the new state, and merge-on-read does not remove conflicts on the same rows. ON t.id = s.id filter: whole table ON t.region = 'EU' AND t.id = s.id filter: EU partitions 85. A CDC table gets slower every hour. How do you diagnose it? A change data capture table that slows every hour is usually accumulating delete files, so measure which kind is growing, compact it on the partitions that change and commit less often. In the query below, growth in content 1 means position deletes from Spark merges, growth in content 2 means equality deletes, typically from Flink upserts, and shrinking data files mean small files from each batch. Schedule rewrite_data_files with a delete threshold on active partitions, remove dangling deletes and expire snapshots. A longer trigger creates fewer delete files, and equality deletes need the most frequent compaction. Compaction competes with the stream, so use partial progress or compact slightly older partitions. Alert on delete records as a share of data and on compaction failures. Copy-on-write is better when reads dominate, changes sit in few files and batches are large and rare. See CDC into Iceberg. What three merges cost on one table. SELECT content, count(*) AS files, sum(record_count) AS records FROM demo.shop.orders.files GROUP BY content; 86. A query waits a minute before the first task starts. Where do you look? A long wait before the first task starts is planning time, so look at metadata rather than executors. A slow catalog call shows even on tiny tables. A very large metadata JSON points to many retained snapshots, thousands of manifests slow reading the manifest list, overlapping partition ranges stop pruning, many delete files enlarge the delete index and driver garbage collection suggests memory pressure. A filter that cannot be projected onto the partitioning forces every manifest to be read. Rewrite manifests so they cluster by partition, expire snapshots, compact files and commit less often, adding driver memory or distributed planning for very large tables. Compare planning time on the same query before and after, remembering that session caching alone can make a second run fast. The query below sizes the manifests. SELECT count(*) AS manifests, round(sum(length) / 1048576, 2) AS total_mb FROM demo.shop.orders.manifests; 87. Someone ran a DELETE without a WHERE clause an hour ago. How do you recover? To recover from a DELETE without a WHERE, stop writers and maintenance, find and tag the last good snapshot, restore it and verify. Stopping writers keeps the situation simple, and pausing expiry protects the data you need. Find the snapshot in history, confirm it with a time-travel count and tag it. If nothing good was committed afterwards, rollback_to_snapshot is enough. If writers continued, insert the missing rows from the tagged snapshot with INSERT ... SELECT ... VERSION AS OF, because a rollback would also discard their commits. Afterwards reprocess anything that read the empty table. To prevent a repeat, restrict delete rights, require predicates in reviewed jobs, tag checkpoints and keep snapshots longer than it takes to notice. If the snapshot has expired, only object versions or backups can help. SELECT made_current_at, snapshot_id, is_current_ancestor FROM demo.shop.orders.history ORDER BY made_current_at DESC LIMIT 5; 88. A bad batch reached production dashboards. How do you stop it happening again? To stop bad batches reaching dashboards, use write-audit-publish: load into a branch, check it, and move main only when the checks pass. Each run gets its own branch. The audit checks counts, nulls, duplicates and totals against the source, with a few meaningful thresholds agreed with consumers. One owner performs the fast_forward; a failed branch is kept for inspection with a retention limit; and if main advanced meanwhile, the branch is rebuilt or its commit cherry-picked. Dashboards keep reading main, unchanged, so they show the last good state while a load is checked. Publishing several tables is not atomic, so publish in dependency order or have readers use tags. Record check results, and when bad data still slips through, roll back or repair forward and add the missing check. load -> branch "batch_2026_11_26" audit -> counts, nulls, duplicates, totals against the source pass -> fast_forward main to the branch fail -> alert, keep the branch for inspection, main untouched 89. Plan the migration of a very large Hive table to Iceberg with little downtime. Plan the migration of a large Hive table by taking an inventory, rehearsing on a copy, choosing in-place migration or rewrite, cutting over with a rollback plan and starting maintenance at once. Record formats, partitioning, file sizes, writers, readers, engine support and permissions. Rehearse with snapshot and compare counts, aggregates and query plans. In-place migrate needs only a short metadata step but keeps the old layout; a rewrite costs a full copy, so choose it when files are small or partitioning is poor. For little downtime, backfill history partition by partition while the old table serves, apply recent changes, validate and switch. At cutover, pause writers, migrate, validate, repoint jobs and views, and keep the backup table until confidence is established. While a snapshot table exists, deleting source files breaks it, and old Hive-style writers and partition filters need review. Prove correctness with per-partition checksums and important queries. 90. A streaming job creates thousands of small files a day. What do you change? A streaming job’s file count is roughly files per commit times commits per day, so reduce both and compact what remains. For example, 200 write tasks on one partition with 1,440 commits a day produce 288,000 files. Lengthen the trigger to the longest acceptable latency, use hash distribution with fewer shuffle partitions or adaptive coalescing, partition more coarsely and keep late data from spreading across many partitions. The fanout writer avoids a sort at a memory cost but does not itself reduce file counts. Compact partitions older than the active window with partial progress and expire snapshots so storage follows. The query below shows files added per hour, which confirms the effect. If the trigger cannot change, compact continuously or keep a hot append table apart from the optimised table that consumers query. 200 write tasks x 1 partition x 1,440 commits per day = 288,000 files per day SELECT date_trunc('hour', committed_at) AS hour, count(*) AS commits, sum(CAST(summary['added-data-files'] AS INT)) AS files_added FROM demo.shop.orders.snapshots GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1 DESC; 91. A busy table gets 503 Slow Down errors from object storage. What do you do? For 503 Slow Down errors, reduce the number of requests first, mainly by compacting, then spread new files across key prefixes and back off on retries. Find which operations and prefixes are throttled and what changed, such as a new job, many small files or a large expiry deleting everything at once. Compaction and better pruning cut requests, write.object-storage.enabled spreads new files, lower maintenance concurrency softens delete bursts and the file IO’s retry and back-off settings absorb transient throttling. Existing files keep their paths, so layout changes help gradually. More parallelism or immediate retries make throttling worse. One enormous file per partition would reduce requests but hurt selective reads and rewrites, so aim for target-sized files. 92. Queries fail with a missing data file after a cleanup job. How can that happen, and how do you respond? A cleanup job can delete files that are still referenced when retention is too short, table locations are shared, paths do not match or something outside Iceberg removes objects. Typical causes are orphan removal catching files of a write still in progress, one table’s cleanup treating another’s files as orphans, URI scheme mismatches with prefix_mismatch_mode => 'DELETE', a table registered in two catalogs, storage lifecycle rules and manual deletion. Stop cleanup and writers, compare all_data_files with storage to list what is missing, and restore from object versions or backups, the only way to get the exact files back. Otherwise remove the broken references and reload that data from a source, checking every affected snapshot. Prevent it with one location per table, generous retention, reviewed dry runs, bucket versioning, no lifecycle rules on table paths and a job that verifies referenced files exist. 93. Spark and Trino report different counts for the same table. How do you investigate? When Spark and Trino count differently, first make sure both read the same catalog and snapshot, then compare how they handle deletes, types and caching. Check the metadata location and pin both queries to one snapshot ID, watching for caches, branch settings and time travel. If pinned counts then agree, the difference was freshness. If they differ without filters, suspect engine support, often for delete files. If they differ only with filters, look at time zones, timestamp types, case sensitivity, null handling or a pruning defect. Narrow it per partition and then per file until the differing rows appear, reproduce on a small table and check release notes; compacting can remove the problem feature meanwhile. Do not treat total-records in a snapshot summary as truth, because it ignores merge-on-read deletes. SELECT snapshot_id, committed_at, summary['total-records'] AS total_records FROM demo.shop.orders.snapshots ORDER BY committed_at DESC LIMIT 3; 94. One customer produces half of all events. How do you partition? When one customer produces half the events, partition by time plus a bucket on an evenly spread key, and sort by customer within files. Time partitions serve retention and most queries. Bucketing on a high-cardinality key such as the event ID spreads writes, including the large tenant’s, and sorting by customer lets filters on other customers skip files. Bucketing by customer would be a mistake, since all of one customer’s rows hash to one bucket and recreate the skew. Size the bucket count by dividing daily bytes by the target file size. Queries for the large tenant will read many files regardless, while small tenants skip almost everything. Watch write task sizes, as a range shuffle can still skew and adaptive execution may need to split partitions. A separate table behind a view suits a tenant with a completely different volume and access pattern. partition: days(event_ts), bucket(N, event_id) sort: customer_id, event_ts 95. You must change partitioning on a live table. How? Change partitioning on a live table with partition evolution, which affects new writes only and lets old data be rewritten later if needed. Review writers, especially dynamic overwrites, and readers, rehearse on a copy, then apply the change in one statement, such as REPLACE PARTITION FIELD months(ts) WITH days(ts). Verify with the query below that new files carry the new spec ID. There is no downtime, queries plan across both specs and old data keeps its layout. Rewrite old partitions only if queries on them are slow, in batches during quiet periods with where and partial progress, since it costs compute and temporary space; expire snapshots to release the replaced files. Overwrite jobs may now replace more or less than before. To reverse, evolve back; files written meanwhile stay readable. SELECT spec_id, count(*) AS files, sum(record_count) AS records FROM demo.shop.orders.files GROUP BY spec_id; 96. An auditor needs a report exactly as it ran six months ago. Is that possible? An auditor’s six-month-old report can be reproduced only if the snapshot still exists, and normal retention will not keep it that long, so it has to be designed in advance. At each reporting close, tag the snapshot with a long retention or none, record the snapshot ID of every table the report read, keep the query and application version, and note engine settings such as the time zone. Reading by tag also uses that snapshot’s schema. If any one input has expired, reproduction fails. Every tag keeps its files alive, so for many years of history an archive table holding the reported data may be cheaper and clearer. Time travel is neither a backup nor tamper proof, since someone with rights can drop a tag; control those permissions and consider immutable storage if the audit requires it. SELECT name, type, snapshot_id, max_reference_age_in_ms FROM demo.shop.orders.refs; 97. Compaction keeps failing because streaming upserts run continuously. What are the options? When continuous upserts keep breaking compaction, keep compaction away from the files being updated and let it commit in small groups. You can compact only settled partitions, accepting that recent data stays fragmented; use partial progress with small groups so a conflict loses little; run in quiet windows between batches; pause the stream briefly for guaranteed progress; or append raw changes and merge periodically, trading freshness for fewer conflicts. Running compaction between micro-batches in the same application removes the race at some latency cost. If updates hit every partition there are no settled ones, so a layout that concentrates changes in recent data makes everything easier. Check which side fails, make sure a failing stream restarts from its checkpoint, and track delete counts and file sizes rather than job success. 98. A job ends with CommitStateUnknownException. What now? After a CommitStateUnknownException, do not rerun the job yet and do not delete its files. Query the snapshots for a matching application ID, operation, time and record counts, or look for the written keys; streaming writes also record query and epoch IDs. If the commit exists, the write succeeded and downstream steps can continue. If it does not and the catalog is healthy, rerun. If the catalog is still unhealthy, wait and check again. Files from a commit that never happened are collected later by orphan removal. There is no automatic retry because it could write the data twice. Make the next occurrence easy by stamping a batch ID into the snapshot summary with a snapshot-property. write option, merging on a key so reruns are harmless and alerting on this exception separately. SELECT committed_at, snapshot_id, operation, summary['spark.app.id'] AS app_id, summary['added-records'] AS added_records FROM demo.shop.orders.snapshots ORDER BY committed_at DESC LIMIT 10; 99. A replay of a change stream created duplicate keys. How do you clean up and prevent it? To clean up duplicate keys from a replayed change stream, find the affected keys, rebuild the correct rows in one atomic operation and then make the pipeline idempotent. The query below finds the duplicates. Pause the pipeline, build the right version of each key as the newest by the source sequence column, replace the affected keys or partitions in a single commit on a branch, validate counts and uniqueness, and publish. If the duplicates came from one commit with nothing after it, a rollback is simpler. Iceberg does not enforce primary keys, so prevention is the pipeline’s job: deduplicate each batch, merge on the real key, guard updates and deletes with the sequence, keep soft deletes if old inserts can be redelivered, avoid resetting checkpoints casually and alert on duplicates. Where a replay enters a CDC pipeline. SELECT order_id, count(*) AS copies FROM demo.shop.orders GROUP BY order_id HAVING count(*) > 1 ORDER BY copies DESC LIMIT 10; 100. Design the Iceberg settings for a raw, cleaned and reporting pipeline. For a raw, cleaned and reporting pipeline, state volume, latency, update rate, consumers and retention first, then choose a write pattern, layout, row-level mode and maintenance plan for each layer. Raw takes frequent appends, partitioned by ingest day, with settled days compacted and source fields kept so later layers can be rebuilt. Cleaned takes upserts by key, laid out by event time and key, using merge-on-read when updates are frequent, with deletes compacted often. Reporting is rebuilt in batches, sorted by common filters, copy-on-write, and tagged at each publish. Raw feeds cleaned incrementally because it is append only; reporting needs the changelog view or a partition rebuild. All layers need one catalog, a maintenance owner, alerts on file size, deletes, failures and freshness, and a recovery path. To cut cost, start with retention and over-frequent commits. source -> raw (append) -> cleaned (MERGE, deduplicated) -> reporting (publish via branch) Concepts and comparisons 101. What is a data lakehouse, and where does Iceberg fit? A data lakehouse runs warehouse-style workloads, with transactions, schemas and fast SQL, directly on files in cheap open storage instead of copying data into a separate warehouse. A warehouse manages its own storage and gives strong guarantees, mostly to one engine. A plain data lake keeps open files shared loosely by many engines with few guarantees. A lakehouse keeps the open files and lets a table format and catalog provide the guarantees. Iceberg is that table layer: it records which files make up a table and how to change that safely, but it is not the storage, the engine or the permission system. The architecture still needs modeling, data quality, access control and maintenance, otherwise it only gives you transactional messy data.
