Nor must it replace the warehouse, which many platforms keep for low-latency serving. +------------------------------------------------------------+ | Consumers BI, notebooks, ML, applications | | Engines Spark, Flink, Trino, warehouses | | Catalog names, commits, permissions | | Table format Iceberg: snapshots, schema, partitioning | | Files Parquet, ORC, Avro | | Storage object storage or HDFS | +------------------------------------------------------------+ 102. Could you build a lake without a table format? What would you have to solve yourself? You can build a lake without a table format, but you then have to build the guarantees yourself: complete writes, safe concurrency, row deletes, schema changes and history. Hiding partial writes takes staging directories, markers and renames. Two writers need external locks. Deleting one customer’s rows means custom partition rewrites, changing a column means coordinating every reader, reprocessing means keeping copies and planning means listing directories. Iceberg covers these with atomic commits, optimistic concurrency, DELETE, field IDs, time travel and manifests. Plain files are enough for immutable, append-only data with one writer, one reader and partitions written once. The hardest part to build is safe concurrent commits, which on object storage need a compare-and-swap that files cannot provide, so weigh that work against running a catalog and maintenance. 103. How does Iceberg metadata differ from the Delta Lake transaction log? Iceberg keeps a tree of immutable metadata for each snapshot, with a pointer to the current version in the catalog. Delta Lake keeps an ordered log of changes with periodic checkpoints. In Delta, the highest committed log entry is current and a writer commits by creating the next log file, which must not already exist; readers load the checkpoint and later entries before skipping files. In Iceberg, the catalog compare-and-swap is the commit point and planning skips manifests and then files. Iceberg partitions through evolvable transforms and tracks columns by field ID, while Delta uses partition columns, generated columns or clustering, and names unless column mapping is on. Both provide atomic commits and time travel, so the choice usually turns on engines, catalog and platform. Tools can generate one format’s metadata over the other’s files, best treated as read only. Iceberg catalog -> metadata.json -> manifest list -> manifests -> files Delta _delta_log/ 000...000.json, 000...001.json, ..., checkpoint.parquet table state = latest checkpoint + the JSON entries after it 104. How do Iceberg's transactions differ from Hive's transactional tables? Hive transactional tables depend on the metastore’s transaction manager and ORC delta files. Iceberg commits by atomically swapping metadata, which any engine that follows the specification can do. Hive records state in metastore transaction tables and delta directories, uses locks, plans from metastore partitions and file listings and compacts delta files itself. Iceberg keeps state in metadata files and a catalog pointer, validates commits optimistically, plans from manifests, works with Parquet, ORC or Avro and is maintained by procedures run from the engine you choose. Because Hive’s guarantees require every writer to use its transaction manager, support elsewhere is uneven. Iceberg can still use the Hive Metastore, but only to hold the table pointer. A transactional Hive table cannot simply be registered, because its delta files are not plain data files, so compact and rewrite it first. 105. One platform on object storage must serve BI and machine learning. Iceberg, Delta Lake or Hudi? To choose between Iceberg, Delta Lake and Hudi for a platform serving BI and machine learning, decide from the workload: engines, update rate, existing governance and required freshness. Engine support differs most, so list who must read and write. Many independent engines and a vendor-neutral catalog API favour Iceberg, a Spark and Databricks platform favours Delta Lake, and high-rate upserts with incremental pipelines favour Hudi. An existing catalog or governance setup often settles it, and freshness drives the write mode and compaction effort. For reproducible model training, all three offer time travel, and what matters is pinning and retaining the version, for example with an Iceberg tag. Prove the choice with your two hardest workloads on the real engines, measuring performance and operational effort. Metadata translation can postpone the choice, at the price of another moving part. 106. What are the Iceberg equivalents of Delta Lake's OPTIMIZE and VACUUM? Delta Lake’s OPTIMIZE corresponds to Iceberg’s rewrite_data_files, and VACUUM is split between expire_snapshots and remove_orphan_files. Compaction is the rewrite procedure, ZORDER BY becomes a Z-order sort strategy within it, and where Delta writes log checkpoints, Iceberg has rewrite_manifests to reorganise metadata. Expiry deletes files that expired snapshots stop referencing; it never searches for files no snapshot knew about, which is orphan removal’s job. Treating the two cleanup steps as one is the usual mistake. Defaults differ too: Delta retains seven days, while Iceberg keeps five days of snapshots and removes orphans older than three days, a limit that should exceed your longest write. To free space after a large delete, rewrite affected files if deletes are merge-on-read, then expire old snapshots. CALL demo.system.expire_snapshots(table => 'shop.orders', retain_last => 3); CALL demo.system.remove_orphan_files(table => 'shop.orders', dry_run => true); 107. When would you not use Iceberg? Avoid Iceberg when you need row-level transactions, millisecond lookups, only very small simple datasets, or when nobody can run maintenance. An application database belongs in PostgreSQL or similar, with indexes, constraints and row-level latency. High-rate point lookups suit a key-value store, because Iceberg has no row index. A small dataset with one reader needs nothing more than Parquet or a database, event streaming between services belongs in a log such as Kafka, and sub-second, highly concurrent dashboards need a serving store or warehouse. Without anyone to compact and expire, a managed warehouse is safer. Iceberg costs a catalog, maintenance jobs, small-file care for streaming and engine testing, which large analytic history repays. Repeated partial-write incidents, painful schema or partition changes, slow planning from partition counts or a second engine needing the same tables are the signals to adopt it. 108. What is in a snapshot summary, and how do you use it? A snapshot summary is a map of properties recorded with each commit: the operation, counts of files and records added or removed, totals and engine identifiers. Added file and record counts reveal small files per commit; keys such as spark.app.id or flink.job-id identify the writing job; and streaming query and epoch IDs trace a micro-batch. You can add your own values through write options with the snapshot-property. prefix. Which keys exist depends on the operation and engine, and totals count records in data files without subtracting merge-on-read deletes. Within those limits, summaries are the quickest record of what each job did to a table. A batch ID of your own pays off after an unknown commit outcome or a retry, because one query answers whether the batch landed. The query below reads several keys. SELECT committed_at, operation, summary['added-data-files'] AS added_files, summary['added-records'] AS added_records, summary['total-data-files'] AS total_files, summary['spark.app.id'] AS app_id FROM demo.shop.orders.snapshots ORDER BY committed_at DESC LIMIT 5; 109. You moved from daily to hourly partitions. Why do some queries still scan daily files? Queries can still scan daily files after a move to hourly partitions because partition evolution does not rewrite history. Files written under the old spec still cover whole days. The new spec applies to new writes, so the table holds both layouts and planning handles each separately; the query below shows which spec each partition uses. Old files that were clustered by time may still be skipped within a day through their column bounds. If old data is rarely queried by hour, leave it. If a recent window needs hourly pruning, run rewrite_data_files with a where clause and options => map('rewrite-all', 'true'), since well-sized files do not otherwise qualify; check the rewritten count and expire snapshots so storage does not hold both layouts. Rewriting everything is rarely worth the compute, and sorting by timestamp can achieve hour-level skipping instead. before the change spec 0: days(ts) one file may hold 24 hours after the change spec 1: hours(ts) files hold one hour query for one old hour -> must open that day's files query for one new hour -> opens only that hour SELECT spec_id, partition, file_count FROM demo.shop.orders.partitions ORDER BY spec_id, partition LIMIT 10; 110. What are Iceberg's Spark procedures, and how do you call them? Iceberg’s Spark procedures are table operations exposed in the catalog’s system namespace and run with CALL <catalog>.system.<procedure>(name => value), which requires the Iceberg SQL extensions. For snapshots and branches there are rollback, set_current_snapshot, cherrypick_snapshot, fast_forward and publish_changes. Maintenance covers rewriting data files, manifests and position delete files, expiring snapshots and removing orphans. Migration uses migrate, snapshot, add_files, register_table and rewrite_table_path, and analysis includes changelog views, table and partition statistics and ancestors_of. Prefer named arguments and literal values, since a call such as current_timestamp() is rejected, and read the result row, which reports what changed. A procedure that changes nothing matched no files. The same operations exist in the Java actions API, and other engines use their own syntax. CALL <catalog>.system.<procedure>(name => value, ...); CALL demo.system.ancestors_of(table => 'shop.orders'); Engines, APIs and access 111. How does Flink write to Iceberg? Flink writers create files continuously, and the Iceberg sink commits them to the table when a Flink checkpoint completes. Append mode adds data files, overwrite replaces partitions in batch jobs, and upsert mode, keyed on a primary key and requiring format version 2 or later, writes delete files alongside new rows. Upsert and overwrite cannot be combined, and in upsert mode partition source columns must belong to the equality fields. Rows can be hash distributed by partition or equality key, which struggles with skew, or range distributed through an experimental option. Because the checkpoint interval is the commit interval, it sets both freshness and the rate of small files, and upserts produce equality deletes that need regular compaction. If checkpoints succeed but no snapshots appear, inspect committer failures and alert on the time since the last commit. records -> writer tasks -> data (and delete) files checkpoint completes -> committer -> one Iceberg snapshot CREATE TABLE sample ( id BIGINT, data STRING, PRIMARY KEY (id) NOT ENFORCED ) WITH ('format-version' = '2', 'write.upsert.enabled' = 'true'); 112. What can table maintenance break in a running Flink job? Table maintenance can break a running Flink job’s commit tracking and delete data it has not yet committed. Expiring the job’s latest snapshot, identified by flink.job-id in the summary, loses the record of what it committed. Orphan removal with a short age limit can delete files waiting for a checkpoint to commit, and compaction on active partitions conflicts with upserts. So keep each job’s latest snapshot, set the orphan age well beyond the longest checkpoint outage you expect, retain snapshots longer than the longest planned downtime and compact only partitions no longer being updated. The risk shows during recovery: a job stopped for a week may be unable to restart safely if maintenance assumed an hour of lag. Give each table one maintenance owner, whether a scheduled Spark job or post-commit maintenance, so retention is set in one place. 113. How do you use Iceberg from Python without a Spark cluster? PyIceberg lets Python use Iceberg without a Spark cluster. It loads a table from a catalog, plans the scan from metadata and returns Arrow data for pandas or DuckDB. It suits reading filtered slices for analysis or machine learning and inspecting metadata, can handle small appends and overwrites from a service, and is the wrong tool for large joins or compaction. Pass a row filter and the selected columns to the scan so that pruning happens before data reaches memory. One process is limited by memory and by the delete files it must apply, so read only the partitions you need. Supported write operations, delete types, transforms and format versions differ from the Java library and change quickly, so check your release. DuckDB and some warehouses can also read Iceberg directly, with their own limits. catalog (REST, Hive, Glue, SQL) -> table -> scan(filter, columns) -> Arrow, pandas, DuckDB 114. How do you share Iceberg tables with consumers outside your platform or cloud? Share Iceberg tables externally by letting capable consumers read them through a catalog, serving others from a query engine or API, or replicating a published copy. Direct access through a REST catalog with short-lived credentials suits large reads by capable engines, at the cost of egress and version compatibility. A query service helps tools without Iceberg support, while you pay for compute and concurrency. A data API suits applications with small payloads, and a copy gives strict isolation at the price of freshness and duplication. Bucket access alone is a poor option, since storage permissions cannot express table rules and raw files give no consistent view. Decide how consumers authenticate, what they may see, how access is audited and how schema or format changes reach them. Publish a stable view or tagged snapshot so your maintenance does not surprise them. 115. How do JDBC clients and BI tools query Iceberg tables? JDBC clients and BI tools reach Iceberg through a query engine over JDBC or ODBC, because Iceberg has no query server of its own. Trino or Presto serves interactive SQL to many users, a Spark Thrift server reuses Spark SQL logic, a warehouse with Iceberg support fits an existing BI estate and Hive serves existing Hive clients. The engine resolves the table through the catalog and reads the files. The JDBC catalog is a different thing: it stores table pointers in a relational database and runs no queries. Dashboard speed depends mostly on the table: cluster it for the dashboard filters, keep file counts reasonable, expose views as the stable interface and size the engine for concurrency. If queries are slow only from the BI tool, inspect its SQL, since wrapped columns or implicit casts can stop pruning. BI tool --JDBC/ODBC--> query engine --catalog--> Iceberg metadata --> files 116. What is the difference between the REST catalog API and a REST API that serves data? The REST catalog API serves table metadata and commits to query engines. A data API serves rows to applications and is something you design yourself. The catalog follows Iceberg’s REST specification and returns table metadata, file locations and credentials; it never returns query results, and the engine still reads the files. A data API is called by your consumers’ applications and should answer from a query engine or serving store instead of reading files on each request. Expecting rows from the catalog is the common mistake. For a data API, precompute the shapes it needs, paginate, pin each response to a snapshot so pages stay consistent and cache by snapshot ID, comparing it with the table’s current one to invalidate. For millisecond responses, publish results to a key-value or relational store and keep Iceberg as the source of truth. 117. How do you query Iceberg together with data in other systems? To query Iceberg together with data in other systems, either federate the query or move the data into Iceberg. Federation connects several catalogs in an engine such as Trino or Spark, pushes filters to each source where possible and joins the results. It is current and quick to start, but loads the source on every query, performs only as well as pushdown and the slowest side allow and reads each source at a different moment. Ingestion costs pipelines and lags behind the source, in return for controlled extraction, optimised layout and a consistent set of snapshots. Weigh how often the query runs, how much data crosses the network, whether the source can take the load and whether results must be reproducible. A hybrid usually works: federate small reference lookups and ingest large or frequently joined data, since an unpushed filter pulls a whole table. 118. How are access control and encryption handled for Iceberg tables? Access control for Iceberg tables is enforced by the catalog, storage permissions and engines, not by the table format. The catalog decides who may list, read, change or drop tables, storage decides who may touch objects, credential vending issues short-lived table-scoped storage access and engines apply row filters, masks or views. If any identity has broad storage access it can bypass the catalog by reading files, so grant storage access through the catalog. Table encryption needs format version 3 and a supporting release: set a key management service on the catalog and encryption.key-id on the table. Data, delete, manifest and manifest list files are encrypted, the metadata JSON is not, and support depends on the catalog and file format. Storage-side encryption is a simpler, separate layer. Column statistics contain real values, so protect metadata too. 119. How do you replicate Iceberg tables to another region for disaster recovery? To replicate an Iceberg table to another region, rewrite its paths for the new location, copy data before the metadata that references it and register the metadata in the second catalog. A plain directory copy fails because metadata holds absolute paths. Run rewrite_table_path on the primary. It writes rewritten metadata and position delete files to a staging area and lists source and target paths, but copies nothing; skip it only if storage preserves the original paths. Copy data files first, then the rewritten files, register the metadata and validate, and rehearse failover and failback. Bucket replication alone is not enough, since objects arrive out of order and the catalog pointer is not replicated. Define recovery point and time objectives, keep a single writer, and make sure expiry on the primary cannot delete files the secondary needs. primary secondary data + metadata --replicate--> data + metadata (paths rewritten) catalog --register --> catalog entry at a chosen metadata file 120. How do you tune read performance on an Iceberg table? Tune read performance by removing the largest source of wasted reading first, usually in the order partitioning, sort order, file sizes, delete cleanup, manifests and statistics. Partitions that match filters skip whole sets of files, sorting or Z-order makes column bounds selective, larger files and fewer deletes reduce per-file work, rewritten manifests speed planning and column metrics and table statistics help the optimiser. Bloom filters (write.parquet.bloom-filter-enabled.column.<name>) help point lookups, and split size and vectorised reads come last. Work from one slow query: record files scanned, bytes read, planning time and the plan, change one thing and measure again. If every file is still read, the filtered column is neither partitioned nor clustered. Dynamic filtering, storage-partitioned joins and aggregate pushdown vary by engine and version. Design and recovery scenarios 121. Someone deleted a manifest file from storage. Is the data lost? Usually not. A manifest only lists files, so the data files are normally still there. Queries on any snapshot that needs the manifest fail with NotFoundException naming the missing .avro file, while other snapshots read normally. Stop writers and pause maintenance first, because orphan removal could delete data that only the broken snapshot referenced. Best is to restore the exact file from object versioning or backup. Otherwise roll back to the latest snapshot that does not use it, as below, and reload newer data from the source. If neither works, rebuild, preferably by reloading from the source. Salvaging files is delicate, because the data directory also holds replaced and orphan files and add_files imports whole directories without applying delete files, so deleted and duplicate rows come back. Copy only the files known to be live to a staging location and reapply the deletes. Versioned buckets, no lifecycle rules on metadata paths and delete rights limited to maintenance protect against this; a missing data file, unlike a manifest, means missing rows. CALL demo.system.rollback_to_snapshot('shop.orders', <last good snapshot id>); 122. The catalog entry is gone or points to a missing metadata file. How do you recover? If the catalog entry is lost or points to a missing file but the table’s files survive, you can register the table again from a metadata file. Stop all writers, list the metadata/ directory, find the newest valid metadata JSON and confirm that its manifest lists and manifests exist. Register it under a temporary name, validate counts and then swap the name, using the call shown below. Choosing the file is the delicate part. An older one silently loses later commits, and a newer one may come from a commit that failed and was never current. Catalog backups, audit logs and the metadata log inside candidate files are better evidence than the highest version number. Never write through two entries for the same table, and back up catalog state with enough storage history to restore what it references. CALL demo.system.register_table( table => 'shop.orders_recovered', metadata_file => '<full path to the metadata.json>'); 123. A job overwrote a large table with wrong data. How do you restore it? Restore a wrongly overwritten table by rolling back to the snapshot before the bad commit, provided nothing valid followed it. The earlier files remain until snapshot expiry removes them. Pause writers and expiry, find the bad commit in snapshots by operation, time and application ID, check its parent with a time-travel query, roll back and replay the corrected job. If good commits followed, rebuild only the affected partitions from the earlier snapshot and reapply later changes. If the snapshot has expired, restore from backup or reload from the source. The usual cause is static overwrite mode replacing the whole table when one partition was intended. Use dynamic or filtered overwrites, validate on a branch before publishing and fail jobs on a row-count guard. The statements below show the inspection and a timestamp rollback. SELECT committed_at, snapshot_id, parent_id, operation FROM demo.shop.orders.snapshots ORDER BY committed_at DESC; CALL demo.system.rollback_to_timestamp('shop.orders', TIMESTAMP '2026-11-27 08:00:00'); 124. Design a table that serves a near-real-time view and a daily batch report from the same data. To serve both a near-real-time view and a daily report, write the stream into one table, serve the live view from the latest snapshot and run the report from a tag taken at the day’s close. First clarify freshness, whether rows are updated or only appended and whether the report must be reproducible. Commit every minute or few minutes, compact closed partitions to control small files, define a cut-off for late events and keep raw data append only, building a merged table if updates are needed. A single dataset means no second pipeline and no drift between real-time and batch figures. Late data after the report is published under a new tag while the old one preserves what was reported. If the live view needs sub-second latency, serve it from a stream processor or serving store and keep Iceberg for history. events -> streaming writer -> events table (append) |-> live view: latest snapshot |-> daily: tag "close_2026_11_26" -> report scheduled: compaction of closed hours, snapshot expiry, manifest rewrite 125. Design a lakehouse that spans an on-premises cluster and a cloud. For a lakehouse spanning on-premises and cloud, give every table one writer and one authoritative catalog, and replicate curated data between sites. Decide where each table lives and who writes it before choosing tools, and never commit from both sides. Replicate curated tables instead of every raw file, plan for absolute path rewriting, account for network latency and egress on cross-site reads and use one identity and policy model across both. Roll out in phases: replicate first, move readers, then move writers table by table with a way back at each step. Expect the link to fail, one side to upgrade its engine first and maintenance to delete files the other side still reads. Querying a table across sites is possible, but heavy readers are usually better served by a local copy. on-prem sources -> on-prem raw tables | scheduled replication of curated data v cloud tables -> cloud engines and BI 126. Design ingestion into Iceberg from hundreds of source tables. Ingesting hundreds of source tables is mainly an operational problem, so configuration rather than code must scale: drive pipelines from a registry, keep a replayable raw layer with idempotent merges and trigger maintenance from metadata signals. Each registry entry gives a table’s keys, mode, schedule and owner. Compatible schema changes apply automatically and others wait for review, events are appended while frequently updated tables use merge-on-read, commits are batched instead of per record and maintenance responds to file and delete counts. Watch catalog load and spread schedules. One failing source must not block the rest, so group by priority and give each table its own checkpoint or bookmark. Track freshness, lag, file counts, delete share and failed commits for every table. sources -> capture (CDC or batch) -> raw append tables -> merge jobs generated from a registry -> curated tables 127. Design Iceberg storage for many tenants. Design multi-tenant storage by choosing a table per tenant, one shared table partitioned or bucketed by tenant, or a mix based on tenant size and isolation needs. Separate tables give strong isolation, separate retention, keys and restore, but there are many to maintain, which suits a few large or regulated tenants. A shared table is cheap to operate and fits many small tenants, with only logical isolation. A hybrid gives the largest tenants their own tables. In a shared table, bucket on a high-cardinality key to spread writes, sort by tenant so filters skip files and enforce tenant filters through views or engine policies. Report maintenance, quotas and cost per tenant from files and partitions. Removing a tenant then requires deletes, rewrites and expiry, and one that outgrows the table can be copied out, rerouted and verified before deletion. 128. How do you test pipeline changes against production-sized Iceberg data safely? Test pipeline changes on production-sized data by using branches for output checks, pinned snapshots for repeatable input and separate copies for destructive experiments. A branch on the production table hides test writes from readers of main. Time travel gives fixed input for comparing old and new logic. The snapshot procedure rehearses a migration of a Hive or Spark table, not of an Iceberg one, and a copy of representative partitions is safest for DDL or layout changes. A repeatable test pins the inputs, runs both versions, writes to separate branches or tables, compares counts, keys, aggregates and sample differences, then drops the branches. Pinning matters because otherwise differences may come from new data. Branches and snapshot tables share files with their source, so take care with maintenance, and never expire a snapshot table’s files. Access control still applies to test copies. Keep small tests in a local catalog for CI. 129. What do you monitor on an Iceberg platform? Monitor four things on an Iceberg platform: freshness, table health, reliability and cost. Alert when time since the last commit exceeds its target, average data file size keeps falling, the share of delete records or the manifest count climbs, the oldest snapshot exceeds retention, commit failures rise, storage grows without data growth or maintenance is missed or changes nothing. snapshots, files, manifests and all_files supply most of these, and the query below is a starting point. Add catalog latency and error rate. Loop over the catalog, store the results in a monitoring table and let maintenance act on thresholds. Wake someone for freshness and commit failures; leave file and delete trends to scheduled work. SELECT max(committed_at) AS last_commit, count(*) AS snapshots, min(committed_at) AS oldest_snapshot FROM demo.shop.orders.snapshots; 130. Storage and compute costs for the lakehouse doubled. Where do you look? When lakehouse costs double, attribute cost per table first, then reduce retained history, wasted rewrites, small files and unnecessary scanning. Look for data reachable but not current and shorten retention or drop references, remove orphans and old object versions, drop duplicated layers, scope and slow compaction that rewrites the same data, fix writers producing small files, improve partitioning, sorting and statistics for queries that scan too much and use merge-on-read or clustering where tiny changes rewrite large files. Weigh both sides, because compaction spends compute to save query compute and requests, and aggressive maintenance on a rarely read table can cost more than it saves. Report per table and owner so the largest consumers are visible and someone can decide on retention. Internals, concurrency and streaming 131. How does schema evolution work inside structs, lists and maps? Schema evolution works inside structs, lists and maps because every nested field has its own field ID. You can add, rename, widen and drop nested fields without rewriting data, except that you cannot add a field to a map’s key struct. Nested fields are addressed by a dotted path, with element naming the struct inside a list and value the struct inside a map. Reading by ID keeps old files compatible: a field missing from a file is filled with null or its default, and one no longer in the schema is skipped. In the example below, addr.city is dropped and added again, so the final query returns NULL although the old file holds Pune; the new field has a new ID. A query on an earlier snapshot still shows the old structure. DROP TABLE IF EXISTS demo.shop.nested PURGE; CREATE TABLE demo.shop.nested ( id INT, addr STRUCT<city: STRING, zip: INT>, tags ARRAY<STRUCT<k: STRING>>, attrs MAP<STRING, STRUCT<a: INT>> ) USING iceberg; INSERT INTO demo.shop.nested VALUES (1, named_struct('city', 'Pune', 'zip', 411001), array(named_struct('k', 'x')), map('p', named_struct('a', 1))); ALTER TABLE demo.shop.nested RENAME COLUMN addr.zip TO postcode; ALTER TABLE demo.shop.nested ALTER COLUMN addr.postcode TYPE BIGINT; ALTER TABLE demo.shop.nested ADD COLUMN tags.element.v INT; ALTER TABLE demo.shop.nested ADD COLUMN attrs.value.b STRING; ALTER TABLE demo.shop.nested DROP COLUMN addr.city; ALTER TABLE demo.shop.nested ADD COLUMN addr.city STRING; SELECT * FROM demo.shop.nested; 132. What is the VARIANT type, and what does shredding do? variant is a format version 3 type that stores semi-structured values such as JSON in a binary encoding. Shredding writes frequently occurring paths into their own typed Parquet columns, so a reader can fetch a path without decoding the whole value. The engine needs a variant type of its own: a Spark 4 build with the matching Iceberg runtime can use it, while Spark 3.5 cannot create such a column. Shredding is off by default and can be enabled by table property, session setting or write option. Rare paths, or ones whose type changes, stay in the binary value. This sits between a JSON string, which must be parsed on every read, and a struct, which is fast but needs a schema change for each new field. Pruning on shredded paths depends on engine and release, so measure bytes read. CREATE TABLE demo.shop.events (id BIGINT, payload VARIANT) USING iceberg TBLPROPERTIES ('format-version' = '3', 'write.parquet.shred-variants' = 'true'); INSERT INTO demo.shop.events SELECT id, parse_json(concat('{"user":', id, ',"city":"Pune"}')) FROM range(100); SELECT variant_get(payload, '$.city', 'string') FROM demo.shop.events WHERE variant_get(payload, '$.user', 'int') = 7; 133. Can two concurrent jobs insert the same key? How do you enforce uniqueness? Yes, two concurrent jobs can insert the same key, because Iceberg enforces no primary key. Two appends succeed, and so do two MERGE statements that only insert; only a MERGE that also has WHEN MATCHED rejects the second writer under serializable isolation. The reason is how each commits. In Spark, a MERGE with only WHEN NOT MATCHED runs as a plain append, which validates nothing against other writers at any isolation level. With WHEN MATCHED it is a row-level operation: serializable isolation checks for newly added files that could match, and the loser gets ValidationException, while snapshot isolation skips the check and both insert. To keep keys unique, use that second form with serializable isolation, rerun the whole statement after a failure and deduplicate the source. A single writer per key range avoids the race altogether. Alert on duplicate keys either way. ALTER TABLE demo.shop.orders SET TBLPROPERTIES ( 'write.merge.isolation-level' = 'serializable'); 134. What happens if the schema changes while a job is writing? If the schema changes while a job is writing, a running append normally still commits. Its files carry field IDs, so readers map them to the new schema. The writer fixed its schema when it planned the job, and at commit it reapplies its files on the latest metadata. A column added meanwhile reads as null or its default for those rows, a rename has no effect, a widened type promotes older values and a dropped column’s values stay in the file unread. Two racing schema changes behave differently: each is committed once against the metadata it started from, so the loser gets CommitFailedException and must be rerun. Row-level operations validate more than appends, and streaming jobs usually keep their starting schema until restarted, so coordinate breaking changes with writers even though the table stays readable. 135. How does the Flink sink achieve exactly-once delivery into Iceberg? The Flink sink achieves exactly-once delivery with a two-phase commit tied to checkpoints: writers close files when a checkpoint starts, the file list is saved in checkpoint state and the committer publishes it after the checkpoint completes. Each snapshot records the job ID, operator ID and highest committed checkpoint ID. If the job fails after committing but before learning of success, recovery reads that ID and does not commit those files again. End to end, the Kafka source replays from offsets saved in the same checkpoint, so source position and table move together. This requires checkpointing, a restart from checkpoint or savepoint and a latest commit that expiry has not removed. Duplicates written into Kafka by producers remain and need a key-based merge or upsert. The Kafka Connect sink has its own exactly-once path through Kafka transactions. barrier arrives writers close data and delete files checkpoint state the file list is persisted; Kafka offsets are saved too checkpoint done committer creates an Iceberg snapshot snapshot summary flink.job-id, flink.operator-id, flink.max-committed-checkpoint-id restore commit only checkpoints newer than the recorded ID 136. Design a CDC pipeline from a database into Iceberg for high event rates with low latency. Build a low-latency CDC pipeline by capturing changes with Debezium into Kafka keyed by primary key, writing them with Flink into an append-only changes table and maintaining a current-state table by upsert or frequent MERGE. Start with arithmetic: at 100,000 events per second and a 30 second checkpoint, each commit carries 3 million events and there are 2,880 commits a day, which sets parallelism, file sizes and maintenance. Keying by primary key keeps each row’s changes ordered, the commit interval should be the longest the latency target allows, the current table is bucketed by key and the source log position is kept for deduplication. Visibility is about the commit interval plus commit time. The raw table allows replay after a merge bug, equality deletes need compaction from the first day, and lag, commit time, delete counts and event age need monitoring. database -> Debezium -> Kafka (partitioned by primary key) -> Flink -> changes table (append, partitioned by ingest hour) -> current table (upsert or MERGE, bucketed by key) maintenance: compact deletes and data, expire snapshots 137. Why does Flink write equality deletes instead of finding the old row's position? Flink writes equality deletes because finding an old row’s position would need an index from every key to its file and row. Its writer keeps that map only for rows inserted during the current checkpoint. So a key inserted and then changed within one checkpoint gets a position delete, while a key from an earlier commit gets an equality delete holding just the key. This keeps writer state small and writes fast, and shifts the read cost described in question 47 onto queries until compaction removes the deletes. The alternative builds the index in maintenance. An experimental Flink task reads equality deletes from a staging branch, resolves them through a primary key index in Flink state and commits deletion vectors to the target branch, requiring format version 3. State grows with live rows, so size it generously, prefer RocksDB and avoid other writers on the target. key inserted in this checkpoint, then updated -> position delete (writer knows file and row) key written by an earlier commit -> equality delete (writer knows only the key) 138. Change events arrive out of order or hours late. How do you apply them correctly? Apply late or out-of-order change events by ordering on a sequence from the source rather than arrival time: keep the newest event per key in each batch, apply it only if newer than the stored row and keep deletes soft while old events can still arrive. In the example below, an event for key 1 with sequence 15 arrives after a delete at 30 and changes nothing. Had the row been physically removed, that old event would have found no match and brought the customer back. Readers filter on deleted = false, usually through a view, and soft-deleted rows are purged once older than the longest possible delay. A direct streaming upsert applies events in arrival order, so it is safe only when each key’s events arrive in order, such as through one Kafka partition. Check how far back late events reach, since merging them touches old partitions. DROP TABLE IF EXISTS demo.shop.customers PURGE; CREATE TABLE demo.shop.customers (id BIGINT, name STRING, seq BIGINT, deleted BOOLEAN) USING iceberg; INSERT INTO demo.shop.customers VALUES (1, 'new name', 30, true); MERGE INTO demo.shop.customers t USING ( SELECT id, name, seq, deleted FROM ( SELECT *, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY seq DESC) AS rn FROM VALUES (1, 'late name', 15L, false), (2, 'second', 40L, false) AS v(id, name, seq, deleted) ) latest WHERE rn = 1 ) s ON t.id = s.id WHEN MATCHED AND s.seq > t.seq THEN UPDATE SET * WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *; SELECT * FROM demo.shop.customers ORDER BY id; 139. How do you handle bad or mismatched records without stopping a streaming sink? Handle bad or mismatched records by separating them before the Iceberg sink: validate each one, write good rows to the table and send failures to a dead-letter topic or errors table with enough context to replay them. In Flink this is a side output from the validating operator; in Spark Structured Streaming, a split inside foreachBatch whose two writes must be safe to repeat. Kafka Connect’s error handling covers converter and transform failures, so check what your sink does when a record fails at write time. Once a bad record reaches the writer, a type or schema mismatch usually fails the task, and a restart meets it again, so validate types, required fields and ranges. Alert on the dead-letter rate, stop the pipeline if most records fail and keep a replay job that merges corrected records by key. source -> parse and validate -> valid -> Iceberg table -> invalid -> dead-letter: raw payload, reason, topic, partition, offset 140. How does Spark's AvailableNow trigger work with an Iceberg source? Spark’s AvailableNow trigger processes everything available in the Iceberg source when the query starts, in one or more micro-batches, and then stops. The checkpoint lets the next run continue. Each micro-batch commits its own snapshot to the target, and rate limit options such as maximum files per batch decide how a backlog is divided. A run with no new data commits nothing, and commits arriving after the end point is fixed wait for the next run. This gives scheduled jobs streaming’s bookkeeping without a permanently running cluster. The usual streaming limits remain: overwrite and delete snapshots stop the query unless skipped, and the source must retain snapshots until the next run has read them. The code below shows the pattern. (spark.readStream.format("iceberg") .option("streaming-max-files-per-micro-batch", "100") .load("demo.shop.source") .writeStream.format("iceberg") .trigger(availableNow=True) .option("checkpointLocation", "s3://bucket/checkpoints/target") .toTable("demo.shop.target") .awaitTermination()) 141. How do you handle schema changes automatically in a Kafka to Iceberg pipeline? Automate only additive schema changes in a Kafka to Iceberg pipeline: let the sink add nullable columns, send incompatible records to a dead-letter path and review renames, type narrowing and drops. Kafka Connect can add missing record fields with iceberg.tables.evolve-schema-enabled, Flink’s experimental dynamic sink can update table schemas and Spark can use mergeSchema on tables with write.spark.accept-any-schema. A schema registry with compatibility rules stops most breaking changes at the producer, which is cheaper. Without those rules, a misspelt field becomes a permanent column and a rename appears as a new column beside one that stops filling. Many streaming jobs also fix their parser schema at startup and ignore new fields until restarted, so alert on unknown fields and let someone decide. 142. When would you append to a staging table and merge periodically instead of upserting directly? Append to a staging table and merge periodically when minutes or hours of latency are acceptable and you want cheap reads, replay and control over conflicts. Upsert directly when the table must be fresh within one checkpoint. Direct upserts accumulate equality deletes, order events by arrival, replay from Kafka only while it retains them and conflict with compaction continuously. Staging lets the merge choose its write mode, order and deduplicate by a source sequence, replay from the table and schedule compaction between runs, at the price of storing data twice. The merge reads new staging rows incrementally, which works because that table only receives appends. A mix is common: consumers needing seconds read the append table through a latest-row view, while everyone else reads the merged table. Layout, maintenance and performance 143. What goes wrong when you change identity(region) to bucket(16, region)? Changing identity(region) to bucket(16, region) usually backfires, because bucketing suits columns with many distinct values and a region has few. With eu, us and ap, two of the three fall into the same bucket of 16, leaving only two partitions in use. Old files keep the identity layout and new ones use buckets, so queries are planned against both specs. A filter on region = 'eu' reads exactly that region in old files, but a whole shared bucket in new ones. Range filters stop pruning, deleting a region now rewrites mixed files instead of changing metadata, and dynamic overwrite replaces a bucket that may cover several regions. If the aim was to split one large region into smaller pieces, keep the region partition and add a bucket on a high-cardinality key, or sort by that key within each partition. ALTER TABLE t REPLACE PARTITION FIELD region WITH bucket(16, region); SELECT spec_id, partition, record_count FROM t.files; 144. Linear sort, Z-order or Hilbert curve: which clustering should you use? Use a linear sort when one column dominates the filters, and a space-filling curve (Z-order or Hilbert) when queries filter on two to four columns independently. A linear sort prunes superbly on its leading column and poorly on later ones. A curve spreads locality across columns, giving up some precision on each; Z-order’s jumps widen some file ranges, while Hilbert keeps better locality but has narrower support. Spark’s rewrite_data_files accepts Z-order, and newer releases accept hilbert() on Spark 4.1 and later; on Spark 3.5 it fails with “Cannot convert transform with more than one column reference”. Choose curve columns carefully. A mostly null or single-valued column adds little, a steadily increasing timestamp is usually clustered already by ingestion and partitioning, and only the first 8 bytes of a long string count by default (var-length-contribution). Each extra column weakens the others. CALL demo.system.rewrite_data_files( table => 'shop.orders', strategy => 'sort', sort_order => 'zorder(customer_id, order_id)', options => map('rewrite-all', 'true')); 145. When does bin-pack compaction make queries slower? Bin-pack compaction makes queries slower when it merges files that held different, narrow ranges of a filter column, so that each output covers a wide range and column bounds stop skipping files. Bin-pack combines files by size without clustering data across them. It is the cheapest strategy, with little shuffle. A sort rewrite shuffles and sorts to restore narrow ranges, and Z-order costs the most while narrowing several columns together. The damage appears on tables that were deliberately sorted or whose arrival order clustered a column: planning gets faster with fewer files, yet each query reads more bytes. Use bin-pack where tables are read in full or by partition, and the sort strategy, restricted with where to closed partitions, where speed depends on bounds. Judge the result by bytes scanned, not file counts. before file A: customer 1..10 file B: customer 900..910 filter 905 reads B bin-pack file AB: customer 1..910 filter 905 reads AB 146. How does the Parquet row group size affect pruning and object store reads? The Parquet row group size controls pruning inside a file and how a scan splits it into byte-range requests. Manifest pruning works on whole files and is unaffected. Each row group has its own column statistics. Readers fetch the needed column chunks with ranged reads, and Iceberg records split offsets so that a large file can be divided between tasks at row group boundaries. Smaller groups skip more precisely but add footer metadata and requests. Larger ones compress and encode better and need fewer requests, while using more writer memory for each open file. The property is write.parquet.row-group-size-bytes, 128 MB by default. Wide tables fit few rows into a group, and many open partitions multiply writer memory by that size. Sort the data first, since statistics help little on unclustered data, and change the size only after measuring. 147. How do you optimise a table with hundreds of columns when queries read only a few? Optimise a very wide table by relying on Parquet to read only the projected columns, then controlling the costs that grow with width: statistics, footers, write memory and rows per row group. Bounds are collected for the first 100 columns by default, so a filter column beyond that cannot skip files until you set write.metadata.metrics.column.<name>. If manifests are large, set the default mode to none or counts and enable only filter columns. Publish views to discourage SELECT *, limit partitions per write task, and group sparse, changing attributes in a struct, map or variant. Sort on common filter columns so their bounds are selective. Rarely used columns that bloat rewrites can move to a second table with the same key, but that adds a join, so split only when the column groups are really used apart. 148. How would you automate maintenance for thousands of tables? Automate maintenance across thousands of tables with a control plane that reads each table’s metadata, scores the work worth doing and runs it within a compute budget, skipping tables that have not changed and have no problem. A registry holds owner, tier and retention. Signals come cheaply from metadata tables, as in the query below: small files, delete files and average size. Rank higher the frequently queried partitions with many small files, growing delete counts and tight targets; rank lower unread tables, tables with no new snapshot and rewrites that move much data to save few files. Compact only qualifying partitions with where, run expiry and orphan removal from each retention policy, allow one maintenance job per table and record before and after values. That record shows whether the spend helped and exposes jobs that keep selecting nothing or losing conflicts. registry (owner, tier, retention) -> collect signals -> score -> queue -> workers with a concurrency limit, one maintenance job per table -> record results SELECT count(*) AS files, sum(CASE WHEN file_size_in_bytes < 134217728 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS small_files, sum(CASE WHEN content <> 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS delete_files, round(avg(file_size_in_bytes) / 1048576, 2) AS avg_mb FROM demo.shop.orders.files; 149. How do you stop rewrite_data_files from running out of memory on very large tables? Stop rewrite_data_files running out of memory by bounding how much is in flight: smaller file groups, fewer groups at once, a where clause and partial progress. max-file-group-size-bytes (100 GB) sets each unit of work and max-concurrent-file-group-rewrites (5) how many run together. With partial-progress.enabled, finished groups commit early, in at most partial-progress.max-commits (10) commits, and partial-progress.max-failed-commits, equal to that by default, sets the failures tolerated. Sort and Z-order rewrites shuffle and need far more memory and disk than bin-pack; shuffle-partitions-per-file spreads each output over more partitions. Many delete files add memory to every task. A partial-progress job can finish with only part of its selection rewritten, so check failed_data_files_count and rerun. min-input-files changes which groups qualify, not their memory use. CALL demo.system.rewrite_data_files( table => 'shop.orders', where => 'order_ts < TIMESTAMP \'2026-11-04 00:00:00\'', options => map( 'max-file-group-size-bytes', '10737418240', 'max-concurrent-file-group-rewrites', '2', 'partial-progress.enabled', 'true', 'partial-progress.max-commits', '10')); 150. rewrite_manifests ran, but planning is still slow. Why? Planning can stay slow after rewrite_manifests because the rewrite helps only when the number or arrangement of manifests was the problem. It cannot fix filters that do not prune, large metadata files, many delete files or a slow catalog. Check whether manifests are ordered by a column queries filter on, using sort_by to choose it, and whether the filters can be projected onto the partitioning. A huge metadata file calls for expiry, delete files for compaction and streaming writes can fragment manifests again soon after. Driver garbage collection points to memory. commit.manifest.target-size-bytes, 8 MB by default, sets manifest size: larger ones mean fewer to open but coarser skipping. The procedure’s use_caching argument only caches data inside the rewrite job and does nothing for later planning. CALL demo.system.rewrite_manifests( table => 'shop.orders', sort_by => array('order_ts_day')); 151. How do you fix driver out-of-memory errors during scan planning? Fix driver out-of-memory errors in planning by shrinking the metadata the driver holds or spreading planning across the cluster. The usual cause is a scan over very many files, each with statistics for many columns, some with deletes. Filters on partition and sort columns load fewer manifests, compaction removes file entries, limiting metrics to filter columns makes entries smaller, delete compaction shrinks the delete index and rewritten manifests skip better. Setting read.data-planning-mode to distributed has executors read manifests; the default is auto. Finally, give the driver more memory. Distributed planning still returns results to the driver, so spark.driver.maxResultSize can be the next limit. Confirm that planning is what fails, meaning the error precedes any scan task. Question 86 covers slow but successful planning. 152. A Trino query filtered on the partition column still scans tens of thousands of files. How do you diagnose it? When a Trino query filtered on the partition column still scans tens of thousands of files, work from the table outwards: count the files that really match, check their partition spec and see whether the filter reached the Iceberg scan. The query below, or Trino’s "orders$files" and "orders$partitions" tables, shows the layout. If the partition truly holds that many files, compact. Files under an old or unpartitioned spec are left over from evolution. A wrapped or cast column may not push down, a literal with a different type or time zone widens the range, a filter arriving through a join depends on dynamic filtering and a second filter on an unsorted column cannot skip files whose bounds all overlap, so cluster on that column. Use EXPLAIN for the scan constraint and EXPLAIN ANALYZE for what was read, then retest with a literal on the raw column. If the file count drops, rewrite the query or the view that generated it. SELECT spec_id, partition, count(*) AS files FROM demo.shop.orders.files GROUP BY spec_id, partition ORDER BY files DESC LIMIT 10; 153. Does a filter such as CAST(event_ts AS DATE) still prune partitions? In Spark 3.5, CAST(event_ts AS DATE) and to_date still prune, because they are rewritten into a timestamp range. date_trunc and date_format on the column are not pushed to the Iceberg scan. In the first plan below, the cast appears as a range on the timestamp in the filters= list of the BatchScan node, and to_date behaves the same way. The second plan, with date_format, shows only a not-null check, and date_trunc gets no range filter either, so every file is considered and Spark filters rows afterwards. These rewrite rules differ between engines and versions, so read the plan instead of assuming. The portable form compares the raw column with literal bounds, such as order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2026-11-02' AND order_ts < TIMESTAMP '2026-11-03', remembering that the session time zone decides which instants those literals mean. EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM demo.shop.orders WHERE CAST(order_ts AS DATE) = DATE '2026-11-02'; EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM demo.shop.orders WHERE date_format(order_ts, 'yyyy-MM-dd') = '2026-11-02'; 154. A MERGE updating ten thousand rows in a huge table takes hours. How do you fix it? A MERGE that updates ten thousand rows but takes hours is probably scanning and rewriting far more than it changes. Without a predicate limiting the target, every file is a candidate. Copy-on-write rewrites each file holding even one match, so ten thousand rows spread over as many 512 MB files means rewriting about 5 TB. Put a literal partition range, computed from the source, in the ON clause, as below. Cluster the table on the merge key so matches fall in few files, use merge-on-read, deduplicate and filter the source so it may broadcast, or partition both sides compatibly to avoid a shuffle. Spark’s runtime row-level group filter, on by default, reduces rewritten files, but the matching join still reads whatever static predicates allow. Compare files scanned and written in the Spark UI and look for spill. CREATE OR REPLACE TEMPORARY VIEW order_updates AS SELECT order_id, 'PAID' AS status, max(order_ts) AS order_ts FROM demo.shop.orders WHERE order_id < 10 GROUP BY order_id; MERGE INTO demo.shop.orders t USING order_updates s ON t.order_id = s.order_id AND t.order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2026-11-01 00:00:00' AND t.order_ts < TIMESTAMP '2026-11-06 00:00:00' WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET status = s.status; 155. Do delete files turn off vectorized reads? Delete files do not turn off vectorized reads for Parquet in Iceberg’s Spark reader, although they do rule them out for ORC. Spark batch reads use the vectorized Parquet reader when it is enabled, the projected columns are primitive and all files are Parquet, with or without deletes. Projecting a struct, list or map, or mixing file formats, falls back to row reads, as does ORC with delete files. read.parquet.vectorization.enabled is true by default, while ORC vectorization is off. So a slow table with deletes is usually paying to load and apply them, particularly equality deletes, rather than suffering a change of reader; check delete counts and compact. These rules describe one release of the Spark connector. Trino and other engines have their own readers, so confirm their behaviour from plans and statistics. 156. Object storage request costs are high although queries return little data. Why? Object storage request costs can be high on small results because each query and job requests metadata and file ranges before returning anything. The count follows files, delete files and planning passes, not result size. Many small data files, each with a footer and column ranges, are cured by compaction, and delete files by delete compaction. Heavy planning calls for manifest rewrites and table caching, constant polling for longer intervals or cached results and useless filters for better partitioning and sorting. Run orphan removal, which lists whole prefixes, less often and more narrowly, and commit less often. Measure first with access logs or request metrics grouped by prefix, operation and identity, to see whether data, metadata or listings dominate. A very short or disabled catalog cache trades request cost for freshness. 157. ZSTD or Snappy for Iceberg data files? ZSTD is the default for new Iceberg tables and usually produces much smaller files, while Snappy uses less CPU. On object storage, where network reads are often the bottleneck, smaller files tend to win. The ratio depends heavily on content: for one synthetic table of a million rows with repetitive strings, ZSTD wrote about 1.9 MB and Snappy about 6.0 MB. ZSTD therefore saves storage and bytes read, costs more write CPU and offers tunable levels. Measure with your own data by writing the same sample with both codecs and recording file size, write time and real query time on your engines. The property affects only files written afterwards, and old files keep their codec until a rewrite touches them, so a mixed table is normal and readable. ALTER TABLE t SET TBLPROPERTIES ('write.parquet.compression-codec' = 'snappy'); Catalogs, governance and migration 158. How do Hive Metastore, AWS Glue, Nessie, Polaris and Unity Catalog compare as Iceberg catalogs? Hive Metastore, AWS Glue, Nessie, Apache Polaris and Unity Catalog can all hold the pointer to an Iceberg table’s metadata; they differ in protocol, access control, features and operator. Hive Metastore speaks Thrift and is already present on Hadoop platforms, with scaling and coarse security as concerns. Glue is managed and tied to AWS permissions. Nessie adds branches and tags across tables but is another service to run. Polaris speaks Iceberg REST, grants privileges to roles and vends short-lived credentials. Unity Catalog exposes a REST endpoint where Databricks documents external read and write for managed Iceberg tables, and read only for foreign Iceberg and Delta tables exposed as Iceberg. Decide on engine write support, permissions, commit rate, backup and exit effort, checking current documentation because these products change quickly. Question 49 covers general selection. 159. How does credential vending work in a REST catalog, and what can it not secure? With credential vending, the engine asks a REST catalog to load a table, and the catalog returns short-lived storage credentials limited to that table’s location. The client requests this with the X-Iceberg-Access-Delegation header; the catalog authorises the principal and returns metadata with temporary credentials. Compared with giving engines direct bucket access, which lets them bypass catalog permissions, only the catalog holds broad rights. Remote signing is the alternative in which the catalog signs each request, at the cost of more calls. Scoping per table avoids writing storage policies for every user and table, and long jobs depend on the client refreshing expiring credentials. It cannot restrict rows or columns, since anyone who can read a file reads all of it. Remove engines’ standing bucket permissions and give each table its own prefix. engine -> catalog: load table (header X-Iceberg-Access-Delegation: vended-credentials) catalog: authorises the principal for this table catalog -> engine: metadata + temporary credentials scoped to the table's paths engine -> storage: reads and writes with those credentials 160. What happens if two catalogs point at the same table, and how do you avoid it? If two catalogs point at the same table, each swaps its own pointer and never sees the other’s commits, so the table forks. Changes are lost, and maintenance on one side can delete files the other references. One catalog must own commits, with every engine writing through it and other platforms reading through it or receiving a refreshed read-only copy. Snowflake shows both arrangements: for Snowflake-managed tables it is the catalog, handles maintenance and documents external read and write through the Horizon Iceberg REST API; for externally managed ones another catalog owns the table. Snowflake’s support is then more limited, it must refresh to see changes, and writes are supported for tables in a remote Iceberg REST catalog. Check current limits. Detect a fork by comparing metadata locations. Repair it by stopping writers, choosing the true history, replaying the other’s changes and removing the duplicate without purge. catalog A -> v10 -> writer A commits v11a catalog B -> v10 -> writer B commits v11b both succeed; the histories diverge 161. How do query engines cache Iceberg metadata, and when can results be stale? Engines cache Iceberg metadata safely because metadata files are immutable. Results go stale when an engine caches which snapshot or metadata file is current. Spark’s catalog cache is on by default with a 30 second expiry. Trino’s iceberg.metadata-cache.enabled, also on, keeps metadata files in coordinator memory, or on local disk when the file system cache is used. StarRocks caches in memory and optionally on disk and refreshes in the background by polling the metastore, every ten minutes by default, which can appear directly as lag after another engine commits. When engines disagree, find the snapshot ID each one is using, refresh or restart the lagging cache and compare again. Check the cache settings for your versions, and for results that must match, pin both queries to one snapshot or tag. 162. How do you apply column masking and row-level security consistently across engines? The Iceberg table format defines no row or column policies, so masking and row-level security are enforced by the catalog and engines. Consistency comes from letting only engines that enforce your rules read the files. Per-engine policies drift unless carefully duplicated, and a central policy service covers only engines with its plugin. Views with filters and masks need compatible dialects and denied access to base tables. Masked copies and a query service in front of restricted data work everywhere, at the cost of extra pipelines or a single access path. Credential vending and storage permissions stop at the file: anyone who can read it sees every column and row. Classify data, limit direct file access to trusted jobs, publish masked copies for others, test one user in every engine and remember that statistics reveal values. 163. What can Iceberg's metrics reporting tell you? Iceberg’s metrics reporting produces a report after planning a scan or committing a change. A scan report shows planning time, manifests and data files scanned or skipped and delete files involved. A commit report shows attempts, duration and the files and records added or removed. Reports are only logged by default. Setting the catalog property metrics-reporter-impl to a class implementing MetricsReporter, as below, sends them to your monitoring system, and REST catalogs can receive them from clients. This is a cheap way to see trends across many tables, where rising commit attempts signal contention and a falling share of skipped files signals layout decay. Only clients that report are covered, so combine it with metadata tables, which describe a table whoever wrote it. spark.sql.catalog.prod.metrics-reporter-impl=com.example.PlatformMetricsReporter 164. How do you enforce table standards at creation time? Enforce table standards at creation through catalog configuration: table-default. properties apply when a statement gives no value, and table-override. properties replace whatever it asks for. With the override shown below, a CREATE TABLE that sets the property to false still produces true. Defaults suit sensible starting values that owners may change, while overrides apply to tables created through that configuration. A catalog service policy, where supported, binds every client, and a scheduled audit finds drift. The prefixes are client settings, so an engine configured without them ignores them, and they do not stop a later ALTER TABLE. Pair them with permissions on altering tables and an audit job that reads properties and reports exceptions. spark.sql.catalog.prod.table-default.write.parquet.compression-codec=zstd spark.sql.catalog.prod.table-override.write.metadata.delete-after-commit.enabled=true spark.sql.catalog.prod.table-default.history.expire.max-snapshot-age-ms=604800000 165. What do Apache XTable and Delta UniForm translate, and what is lost? Apache XTable and Delta UniForm both write another format’s metadata over existing data files without copying data. XTable converts between Hudi, Delta Lake and Iceberg, while UniForm goes only from Delta to Iceberg or Hudi. XTable runs as a separate sync step and does not carry over merge-on-read tables or deletion vectors. UniForm generates metadata asynchronously after Delta commits, is read only for the other clients, and its documented Iceberg compatibility version 2 mode excludes deletion vectors. Format-specific features, such as generated columns, may be missing on the target. Treat translated metadata as a read-only view: let only the source format’s writers change and maintain the table, monitor sync lag and check the current limitation list before depending on it. 166. Why can add_files return wrong query results, and how do you guard against it? add_files can return wrong results because it registers existing files from their footer metadata without checking that their schema matches the table, and planning then trusts that metadata. A wrong bound from a faulty writer makes planning skip a file that holds matching rows, silently. Mismatched types or names give errors, nulls or wrong values, adding a file twice with the duplicate check disabled duplicates rows, and expiry may later physically delete the files even if another system uses them. After importing, compare minimum and maximum values read from the data with the bounds in the files table, and filtered counts with the source. A filter returning fewer rows than the same condition applied after a full scan indicates bad bounds. If the files’ history is doubtful, rewrite them so Iceberg computes the statistics. 167. Which legacy Hive data types cause trouble in a migration? The legacy Hive types that cause trouble are CHAR and VARCHAR, which become plain strings, and old INT96 timestamps, which are imported without usable statistics. Both can change query behaviour silently. A CHAR(5) value such as ab depends on its writer: Spark pads it, so WHERE c = 'ab' finds nothing after migration, while Hive’s Parquet writer stores it unpadded, so the padded comparison fails; a table may hold both. VARCHAR loses its length limit. INT96 columns are readable but have no bounds in manifests, and timestamps written under different time zone settings may shift. Check stored lengths, then trim CHAR values while rewriting or fix every comparison. Enforce limits in the pipeline and compare edge values, including old dates, on every engine. Rewriting with rewrite_data_files and rewrite-all restores statistics but not inconsistent strings, which need an explicit transformation. 168. How do you keep Hive and Iceberg consistent if both are written during a cutover? Keep Hive and Iceberg consistent during a cutover by avoiding independent dual writes: have one authoritative write path, derive the other table from it and reconcile every batch. Two separate writes cannot be atomic, so one can fail while the other succeeds and retries then differ. If both must come straight from the source, make each write idempotent per batch, record the batch ID in both and publish it only when both have it. First Iceberg shadows Hive and is validated, then readers move in groups, writes switch to Iceberg with Hive fed from it, and finally Hive is retired. Set an exit criterion, such as a number of reconciled batches, and an end date, because an open-ended dual-write period doubles cost and leaves nobody sure which table is right. source -> authoritative table -> derived copy | | +---- reconcile per batch (counts, key checks, checksums) 169. How do you migrate a Hive table whose partitions live in different buckets or paths? A Hive table with partitions in different buckets or paths can be migrated as it is, because migrate, snapshot and add_files record each file’s full path. The metastore’s partition locations are followed and nothing moves. The work comes afterwards, since the table no longer lives under one directory. Every engine needs read access to every location, orphan removal examines only the table location by default, expiry after migrate can delete replaced files anywhere, lifecycle rules on another bucket may delete needed files, disaster recovery must cover all locations and another system may still own a path. Rehearse with snapshot, list path prefixes from the files table and compare partition counts. If the scatter is a problem, rewrite into the table’s own location over time and remove old data once no snapshot refers to it. 170. Can you convert a Delta Lake table to Iceberg without rewriting data? Yes, within limits, a Delta Lake table can be converted to Iceberg without rewriting data. Iceberg’s Delta Lake module has a snapshot action that builds an Iceberg table over the existing Parquet files and replays the transaction history, leaving the source unchanged. The module is separate from the engine runtimes, and its documentation covers older Delta protocol versions (reader 1, writer 2), so features such as deletion vectors are not included. The files are shared: a VACUUM on the source can break the new table, and expiry or orphan removal on the new table must never run. The documentation prohibits that cleanup, yet the action does not set gc.enabled to false and uses the source location by default, so set both yourself. For a permanent move, stop Delta writers, take the snapshot, validate it and rewrite the data into the new table so that it owns its files. For read access only, use metadata translation. DeltaLakeToIcebergMigrationActionsProvider.defaultActions() .snapshotDeltaLakeTable("s3://bucket/delta/orders") .as(TableIdentifier.of("db", "orders")) .icebergCatalog(catalog) .deltaLakeConfiguration(hadoopConf) .execute(); 171. How do you prove that a migrated table matches its source at large scale? Prove that a migrated table matches its source by freezing or pinning both sides and comparing in layers: counts, per-partition checksums, column aggregates and finally the rows of any partition that differs. The query below sums a hash of every row for each day on both tables and returns only mismatches, so no rows means they agree. Summing hashes ignores row order and still notices duplicates, although matching checksums are strong evidence rather than proof. Cast both sides to identical types, since a type or time zone difference changes hashes even when data is right, and watch nulls and padded strings. Compare a fixed Iceberg snapshot with a quiet source, examine differing partitions with EXCEPT ALL and finish by running the business queries people care about. DROP TABLE IF EXISTS demo.shop.orders_copy PURGE; CREATE TABLE demo.shop.orders_copy USING iceberg AS SELECT * FROM demo.shop.orders; WITH source AS ( SELECT CAST(order_ts AS DATE) AS day, count(*) AS n, sum(CAST(xxhash64(order_id, customer_id, amount, status, order_ts) AS DECIMAL(38,0))) AS h FROM demo.shop.orders GROUP BY CAST(order_ts AS DATE) ), target AS ( SELECT CAST(order_ts AS DATE) AS day, count(*) AS n, sum(CAST(xxhash64(order_id, customer_id, amount, status, order_ts) AS DECIMAL(38,0))) AS h FROM demo.shop.orders_copy GROUP BY CAST(order_ts AS DATE) ) SELECT * FROM source FULL OUTER JOIN target USING (day) WHERE NOT (source.n <=> target.n AND source.h <=> target.h); Operations, recovery and cost 172. A table was dropped with PURGE, but the bucket has versioning. How do you recover it? With bucket versioning, a table dropped with PURGE can be recovered by restoring the deleted object versions and registering the latest metadata file. Pause jobs and lifecycle rules first, then find the table location from catalog logs, backups or job configuration. A versioned delete normally leaves a delete marker, so remove markers or copy previous versions back for the newest metadata JSON, its manifest lists and manifests and every data and delete file they reference. Register it under a temporary name, as below, validate counts and rename. Anything a lifecycle rule has already removed is gone, so the retention of old versions is the real recovery window. Files outside the table location need restoring too. Rehearse on a test table, because restoring millions of objects takes planning and time. CALL demo.system.register_table( table => 'shop.orders_restored', metadata_file => 's3://bucket/warehouse/shop/orders/metadata/<latest>.metadata.json'); 173. A pipeline bug corrupted hundreds of related tables. How do you restore them to one point in time? To restore hundreds of related tables to one point, roll each back to the snapshot current at a chosen time, in dependency order with writers stopped, since Iceberg has no cross-table transaction. Stop writers, expiry and orphan removal, pick the moment before the first bad write, find each table’s snapshot in history, record the plan and roll back as below. Then reset bookmarks, streaming checkpoints and source offsets and validate relationships between tables before restarting. A timestamp only approximates consistency because tables commit at different moments; restore by batch ID, or tag a consistent set after each good run. Retention must exceed the time needed to detect such a bug. Generate the calls with a script, review them and keep the previous snapshot IDs so the restore can be undone. CALL prod.system.rollback_to_timestamp('db.orders', TIMESTAMP '2026-11-26 02:00:00'); CALL prod.system.rollback_to_timestamp('db.customers', TIMESTAMP '2026-11-26 02:00:00'); 174. How would you attribute lakehouse storage, compute and request costs to business teams? Attribute lakehouse costs by giving every table an owner, measuring storage from metadata, tagging compute with table and team and taking request costs from access logs by table prefix. The query below sizes everything reachable from any snapshot, using distinct paths because all_files repeats them. Charge storage and maintenance compute to the table owner, query compute to the team that ran it from engine history, requests by prefix and identity and the shared catalog by an agreed rule. Metadata cannot see orphans or old object versions, so reconcile with the storage inventory and report the gap as unowned. For shared tables, allocate storage by tenant partition and query cost by caller. Publish figures alongside the lever each owner controls, such as retention, so the report leads to action. SELECT count(*) AS files, sum(file_size_in_bytes) AS reachable_bytes FROM (SELECT DISTINCT file_path, file_size_in_bytes FROM demo.shop.orders.all_files) f; 175. Can you move old Iceberg data to colder storage classes? Old Iceberg data can move to colder storage classes only if they still allow immediate reads, because every referenced file must be readable at once. Standard and infrequent access classes work, some with retrieval fees, and Glacier Instant Retrieval gives millisecond access at higher retrieval cost and a minimum duration. Intelligent-Tiering’s automatic tiers are fine, but its optional archive tiers need a restore, as do Glacier Flexible Retrieval and Deep Archive, which would break queries, compaction and time travel. Age-based lifecycle rules are risky since an old file may be current, and path rules fail with the object storage layout. Prefer tags set by a process that understands the metadata, never tier metadata files and remember that rewriting cold data pays retrieval. Rarely read data may belong in an archive table. 176. How do you audit who changed or read a table? Auditing who changed or read a table means combining several sources, because table metadata is not an audit log. snapshots and history show what changed and when, summary keys such as application IDs show which job did it, the catalog’s audit log shows which identity committed or loaded the table and engine and storage logs show who read the data. Summaries are written by clients, so they are informative rather than tamper proof, reads leave no trace and expiry removes history. Require jobs to stamp identity and run ID using the snapshot-property. write option, ship catalog and storage logs somewhere writers cannot modify and export snapshot records before they expire. Direct file access bypasses catalog logging, so route access through the catalog. 177. Which rules would you enforce from the start on a company-wide Iceberg platform? On a company-wide Iceberg platform, enforce from the start the rules that are cheap early and very expensive to add later. Each table should have one catalog owning its commits, preventing forks and lost writes. Storage access should come through the catalog, with one location per table, preventing bypassed permissions and cross-table deletion. Every table needs an owner, retention and maintenance from creation, writes should be idempotent with a run ID, and versioned storage, catalog backups and rehearsed restores should make incidents reversible.
