Summary Further reading Trademarks Spark 4.0 is a break with the past and a step forward in the same release. Scala 2.12 and JDK 8 and 11 are gone, ANSI mode is the default so bad data stops a job instead of turning into NULL, and SQL picks up the pieces it was missing: a type for JSON, functions, variables, collations and a query syntax you can read top to bottom. The release notes put 4.0.0, out on 23 May 2025, at over 5,100 resolved tickets from more than 390 people. It’s the first release of the 4.x line and the one every later 4.x release builds on, so it’s where to start if you’re meeting Spark 4 for the first time or planning a move from 3.x. Below are ten features. Each one shows the code you’d have written before 4.0, the code you write now, and what it needs before it works. If a term is new, the glossary covers it. The upgrade section, near the end, is the one to read if you’re coming from 3.x. The features-by-release post lines up all the Spark 4 releases, and Spark 4.1 is the release that follows this one. Image 1: Spark 4.0.0 in numbers, and what the release is about. Image 2: Spark 4.0 by area, with what each feature replaces and what you write now. Key takeaways ANSI mode is on by default. A bad cast or a divide by zero now raises an error, and try_cast and try_divide give you NULL when that’s what you want. This is the change most likely to turn a green pipeline red. Scala 2.13 and Java 17 are the baseline, so every jar your jobs depend on needs a Scala 2.13 build. SQL gets VARIANT, user-defined functions, session variables, collation and pipe syntax, all without a flag. The built-in XML source and the Python Data Source API replace a dependency and a Scala connector. transformWithState lets you keep custom per-key state in a stream, and a state data source lets you read it back. Features at a glance Feature Area On by default? How to turn it on ANSI mode SQL Yes spark.sql.ansi.enabled=false turns it off VARIANT Types Yes Nothing SQL pipe syntax SQL Yes Nothing SQL user-defined functions SQL Yes Nothing Session variables SQL Yes Nothing String collation Types Yes Nothing XML data source and functions Formats Yes Nothing Python Data Source API Python Yes PyArrow installed GROUP BY on maps, DESCRIBE ... AS JSON SQL Yes Nothing transformWithState Streaming Yes RocksDB state store, PyArrow, pandas, protobuf and gRPC Before you start What you need Need Detail Java 17 or 21, per the Spark 4.0.5 overview; 17 is the baseline for 4.0. The apache/spark:4.0.5-python3 image ships Java 17 Scala 2.13. Every jar your jobs depend on needs a Scala 2.13 build Python, for PySpark 3.9 or newer, the lowest floor of the Spark 4 releases Spark pip install pyspark==4.0.5, the apache/spark:4.0.5-python3 image, or the 4.0.5 release tarball PyArrow and pandas For features 8 and 10: pip install "pyspark[sql]" brings them protobuf and gRPC packages For feature 10: pip install protobuf grpcio grpcio-status googleapis-common-protos The RocksDB state store For feature 10: set spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.providerClass to RocksDBStateStoreProvider plotly Only to try the plotting API in the smaller additions Install Spark 4.0 You’ve got two ways in. 4.0.5 is the latest 4.0 release (4.0.0 shipped on 23 May 2025 and 4.0.5 on 27 October 2026). Option 1: pip. The wheel bundles Spark, so you need Java (17 or 21) and Python 3.9 or newer. The sql extra adds PyArrow, pandas and NumPy. python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate pip install "pyspark[sql]==4.0.5" python -c "import pyspark; print(pyspark.__version__)" The last command prints 4.0.5. Point PYSPARK_PYTHON at the same interpreter if your shell’s python3 is a different one, because the workers use it. Option 2: the release tarball in a common path. Download it, check the checksum, unpack it under /opt and point SPARK_HOME at a stable link. curl -LO https://archive.apache.org/dist/spark/spark-4.0.5/spark-4.0.5-bin-hadoop3.tgz curl -s https://archive.apache.org/dist/spark/spark-4.0.5/spark-4.0.5-bin-hadoop3.tgz.sha512 shasum -a 512 spark-4.0.5-bin-hadoop3.tgz # compare with the line above sudo tar -xzf spark-4.0.5-bin-hadoop3.tgz -C /opt sudo ln -sfn /opt/spark-4.0.5-bin-hadoop3 /opt/spark export SPARK_HOME=/opt/spark PATH=/opt/spark/bin:$PATH spark-submit --version The file is 549,108,494 bytes (about 524 MiB). Add the two export lines to ~/.zshrc or ~/.bashrc to keep them. If the version printed isn’t 4.0.5, an older SPARK_HOME in your shell is winning; start with env -u SPARK_HOME. Glossary Term Meaning ANSI mode Spark follows the SQL standard for errors: a bad cast or a divide by zero raises instead of returning NULL try_ function A variant such as try_cast that returns NULL on bad input instead of raising UDF User-defined function: a function you write yourself UDTF User-defined table function: returns several rows per call Collation A rule for how strings compare and sort, such as case-insensitive Session variable A typed value that lives for the session, set with DECLARE and SET VAR VARIANT The Spark type for semi-structured data such as JSON, encoded once in binary rowTag The XML element that the XML reader treats as one row State What a streaming query remembers per key between micro-batches 1. ANSI mode on by default Since: 4.0.0 · Area: SQL · Source: SPARK-44444 Lineage: ANSI mode existed as a setting, off by default; 4.0 flips the default. Until 4.0, a bad cast or a division by zero quietly gave you NULL and the job carried on. That’s friendly right up to the day you notice a column that’s been NULL for a month. In 4.0 spark.sql.ansi.enabled is true by default (SPARK-44444), so the same statements raise an error and the query stops. The message names the fix: use try_cast or try_divide where NULL was what you wanted all along. It’s a good change and a disruptive one. A pipeline that used to finish with some nulls in it may now fail on its first bad row, which is the point, but it still means you should run your real data through a 4.0 cluster before you upgrade. Before Spark 4.0 With ANSI off, which was the 3.x default, both bad inputs came back as NULL. Runnable file: 14_ansi_mode_before.sql. SET spark.sql.ansi.enabled=false; SELECT CAST('abc' AS INT) AS bad_cast, 1/0 AS div_zero; -- NULL, NULL Image 3: The same two statements, with ANSI off and with the 4.0 default. With Spark 4.0: sample code Runnable file: 01_ansi_mode.sql. SET spark.sql.ansi.enabled; -- true SELECT try_cast('abc' AS INT); -- NULL SELECT try_divide(1, 0); -- NULL -- these two fail on purpose: SELECT CAST('abc' AS INT); -- [CAST_INVALID_INPUT] SELECT 1/0; -- [DIVIDE_BY_ZERO] When it fits, and when it doesn’t Leave it on. It’s what makes bad data visible, and the try_* functions are there for the places where NULL is the right answer. Turn it off only as a stopgap while you fix the data, with spark.sql.ansi.enabled=false. Other ANSI behaviour, overflow for example, changes too, so test with your own data and not a toy table. Image 4: Bad rows used to slip through as NULL. Now they stop the query. 2. VARIANT Since: 4.0.0 · Area: Types · Source: SPARK-45827 Lineage: new in 4.0. VARIANT is a Spark type for semi-structured data such as JSON (SPARK-45827). parse_json turns a string into one, stored in a binary encoding so it’s parsed once and not on every read. variant_get pulls a value out by path and gives it back as the type you ask for, and schema_of_variant tells you the shape Spark found. The difference from the old approach is the type. get_json_object always returns a string, so you cast it yourself. variant_get(v, '$.b[1]', 'int') returns an int. Before Spark 4.0 You stored JSON as a string column and read fields with get_json_object, which returns text. Runnable file: 15_variant_before.sql. SELECT typeof(get_json_object('{"a":1,"b":[1,2,3]}', '$.b[1]')) AS before_type; -- string Image 5: A string you cast yourself becomes a typed value. With Spark 4.0: sample code Runnable file: 02_variant.sql. SELECT parse_json('{"a":1,"b":[1,2,3],"c":{"d":"x"}}') AS v; SELECT variant_get(parse_json('{"a":1,"b":[1,2,3]}'), '$.b[1]', 'int'); -- 2 SELECT schema_of_variant(parse_json('{"a":1,"b":[1,2,3]}')); -- OBJECT<a: BIGINT, b: ARRAY<BIGINT>> When it fits, and when it doesn’t Use it for payloads whose shape changes from row to row, such as events with different fields, where a fixed schema would either drop data or fill up with nulls. If the shape is fixed, a typed struct is easier to filter and document. The path syntax in 4.0 is variant_get with a path string and a type string. Image 6: Parse once, then read typed values out of the binary encoding. 3. SQL pipe syntax Since: 4.0.0 · Area: SQL · Source: SPARK-49555 Lineage: new in 4.0. Ordinary SQL starts with SELECT, but you think about a query starting from the table. Pipe syntax (SPARK-49555) lets you write it that way: start with FROM, then chain steps with |>, each one taking the result so far and doing one thing to it. You can still mix it with ordinary SQL, and it compiles to the same plans. It reads like a DataFrame chain, which is a big part of its appeal. There’s less nesting, and you can comment out a step to see what the query did before it. Before Spark 4.0 The same query written the usual way, with SELECT first and the filter and grouping after it. Runnable file: 16_pipe_syntax_before.sql. SELECT region, sum(amount) AS total FROM orders WHERE amount > 5 GROUP BY region ORDER BY total DESC; -- eu 40.0, us 20.0 Image 7: The same query, written in the order you think about it. With Spark 4.0: sample code Runnable file: 03_pipe_syntax.sql. FROM orders |> WHERE amount > 5 |> AGGREGATE sum(amount) AS total GROUP BY region |> ORDER BY total DESC; -- eu 40.0, us 20.0 FROM orders |> EXTEND amount * 2 AS doubled |> SELECT id, doubled |> LIMIT 2; When it fits, and when it doesn’t It’s a good fit for exploratory queries and for long chains of filters and aggregates, where each step is easy to read on its own line. It isn’t a different engine, so a query that’s slow in ordinary SQL is slow here too. Teams that share query templates may want to pick one style, since mixing both in a codebase is allowed but not always pleasant. Image 8: Each pipe takes the result so far and does one thing to it. 4. SQL user-defined functions Since: 4.0.0 · Area: SQL · Source: SPARK-46057 Lineage: new in 4.0. You can now write a function in SQL, scalar or table-valued, with CREATE FUNCTION (SPARK-46057). The body is a SQL expression or query, and Spark inlines it into the plan of the query that calls it, so there’s no trip to a Python worker. In the plan, the Python version shows a pythonUDF0 node, and the SQL version shows only the scan, because the expression got folded in. A table function returns rows, so it can sit in a FROM clause. It’s close to a parameterised view. Before Spark 4.0 For logic you wanted to reuse, a Python UDF was the usual answer, with all the overhead of a Python worker. Runnable file: 17_sql_udf_before.py. spark.udf.register("add_tax_py", lambda x: x * 1.18, "double") spark.sql("SELECT id, add_tax_py(amount) AS gross FROM orders").explain() # Project [id, pythonUDF0 AS gross] Image 9: The same calculation, in a Python worker and inlined as SQL. With Spark 4.0: sample code Runnable file: 04_sql_udf.sql. CREATE OR REPLACE TEMPORARY FUNCTION add_tax(x DOUBLE) RETURNS DOUBLE RETURN x * 1.18; SELECT id, add_tax(amount) AS gross FROM orders ORDER BY id; -- 11.8, 23.6, 35.4, 5.9 CREATE OR REPLACE TEMPORARY FUNCTION big_orders(min_amt DOUBLE) RETURNS TABLE (id INT, amount DOUBLE) RETURN SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount >= min_amt; SELECT * FROM big_orders(20.0); -- ids 2 and 3 When it fits, and when it doesn’t Use them for small, reusable calculations that can be written as an expression, and for parameterised queries. They’re not the place for anything that needs a loop, a library or an external call; that’s still a Python UDF’s job. The floating-point output (11.799999999999999 for the first row) is ordinary DOUBLE arithmetic, and you’d round it for display. Image 10: A Python UDF leaves the JVM. A SQL UDF stays in the plan. 5. Session variables Since: 4.0.0 · Area: SQL · Source: SPARK-42849 Lineage: new in 4.0. A session variable is a typed value that lives as long as your session (SPARK-42849). You declare it with DECLARE VARIABLE, change it with SET VAR, and use it in any query by name. Because it has a type, 15.0 is a DOUBLE and not text that gets pasted into the statement. Before this, the usual trick was SET name=value and then ${name} in the query, which is text substitution. It works, but nothing checks the type and it’s easy to get a quote wrong. Before Spark 4.0 A configuration value and ${...} substitution did the job, as untyped text. Runnable file: 18_session_variables_before.sql. SET threshold=15.0; SELECT id FROM orders WHERE amount > ${threshold} ORDER BY id; -- ids 2, 3 Image 11: A pasted value becomes a typed variable. With Spark 4.0: sample code Runnable file: 05_session_variables.sql. DECLARE OR REPLACE VARIABLE threshold DOUBLE DEFAULT 15.0; SELECT id FROM orders WHERE amount > threshold ORDER BY id; -- 2, 3 SET VAR threshold = 25.0; SELECT id FROM orders WHERE amount > threshold ORDER BY id; -- 3 When it fits, and when it doesn’t Use them for parameters you want to change between queries in one session, such as a date range or a threshold. They live in the session only, so they’re no use for sharing a value between applications. A variable is session-scoped, so a new session starts without it, and a DECLARE has to run again. Image 12: Declare once, read it in any query, change it with SET VAR. 6. String collation Since: 4.0.0 · Area: Types · Source: SPARK-46830 Lineage: new in 4.0. A collation is a rule for how strings compare and sort. Spark 4.0 lets you attach one to a string, so case-insensitive comparison is something you declare, not something you fake with lower() on both sides (SPARK-46830). UTF8_LCASE compares ignoring case, and UNICODE_CI is case-insensitive under Unicode rules. collation('x' COLLATE UNICODE_CI) reports the collation name, which shows as SYSTEM.BUILTIN.UNICODE_CI. The practical gain is that the comparison, a DISTINCT or a GROUP BY follows the rule, and the engine knows about it, so it doesn’t have to wrap every column in a function. Before Spark 4.0 You lowercased both sides, and every query had to remember to do it. Runnable file: 19_collation_before.sql. SELECT lower('Apple') = lower('apple') AS eq; -- true SELECT count(DISTINCT lower(n)) FROM names; -- 2 Image 13: The same answers, with the rule declared on the comparison instead of a function on every column. With Spark 4.0: sample code Runnable file: 06_string_collation.sql. SELECT 'Apple' = 'apple'; -- false SELECT 'Apple' COLLATE UTF8_LCASE = 'apple'; -- true SELECT collation('x' COLLATE UNICODE_CI); -- SYSTEM.BUILTIN.UNICODE_CI CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP VIEW names AS SELECT * FROM VALUES ('Ana'),('ana'),('ANA'),('Bob') AS t(n); SELECT count(DISTINCT n COLLATE UTF8_LCASE) FROM names; -- 2 When it fits, and when it doesn’t Use it when case, or accents, shouldn’t matter for a comparison or a group. It’s less useful for data you only display. The usual surprise is that two strings with different collations can’t be compared directly, so choose one for the column and stay with it. Image 14: The rule goes on the comparison, and the engine follows it. 7. The built-in XML data source Since: 4.0.0 · Area: Formats · Source: SPARK-44265, SPARK-44753 Lineage: new in 4.0 as a built-in; earlier versions needed an external package. Spark 4.0 reads and writes XML itself (SPARK-44265), with no extra package to install on every cluster. Two things come with it: a data source, spark.read.format("xml"), with a rowTag option that names the element to treat as one row, and functions for XML held in a string column. from_xml parses it into a struct, to_xml writes one back, and schema_of_xml infers the schema. The source infers a schema from the elements it finds. With the sample document, the inferred schema is STRUCT<age: BIGINT, name: STRING>, with the fields in alphabetical order. The release notes list the XML reader and writer for PySpark and Spark Connect as well. Before Spark 4.0 Without a parser you pulled values out with XPath functions, one at a time. Runnable file: 20_xml_before.sql. SELECT xpath_string('<p><name>Ana</name><age>30</age></p>', 'p/name') AS name, -- Ana xpath_int('<p><name>Ana</name><age>30</age></p>', 'p/age') AS age; -- 30 Image 15: Two separate calls become one parse into a struct. With Spark 4.0: sample code Runnable file: 07_xml_functions.sql. SELECT from_xml('<p><name>Ana</name><age>30</age></p>', 'name STRING, age INT'); -- {Ana, 30} SELECT schema_of_xml('<p><name>Ana</name><age>30</age></p>'); -- STRUCT<age: BIGINT, name: STRING> # read files, one <person> element per row df = spark.read.format("xml").option("rowTag", "person").load("/tmp/xmlin") # age: long, name: string -> (30, 'Ana'), (41, 'Bob') When it fits, and when it doesn’t It fits feeds from vendors or older systems that still speak XML. If the data is already JSON or Parquet, you don’t need it. The classic stumble is leaving out rowTag: the reader needs to know which element is one row. Image 16: A string column becomes a struct, and XML files become a DataFrame. 8. The Python Data Source API and Python UDTFs Since: 4.0.0 · Area: Python · Source: SPARK-44076, SPARK-43797 Lineage: Python UDTFs arrived earlier (SPARK-43797); the Data Source API and polymorphic UDTFs are new in 4.0. You can write a data source in plain Python, register it, and read it by name, from SQL too (SPARK-44076). A data source is two small classes: a DataSource that names it and gives its schema, and a DataSourceReader whose read method yields rows. No Scala connector to build and ship. A Python user-defined table function, a UDTF, returns several rows for each input row. It’s a class with an eval method that yields tuples. Python workers run the reader and the data moves through Arrow, so PyArrow has to be installed. On the official image the data source worker fails with ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pyarrow' until it is. Before Spark 4.0 You built the rows in the driver and handed them to createDataFrame, which only works for data that fits there. Runnable file: 21_python_data_source_before.py. spark.createDataFrame([(i, i * i) for i in range(1, 5)], "n int, square int").show() Image 17: A one-off list on the driver becomes a reusable source with options. With Spark 4.0: sample code Runnable file: 09_python_data_source.py. from pyspark.sql.datasource import DataSource, DataSourceReader class CounterDataSource(DataSource): @classmethod def name(cls): return "counter" def schema(self): return "n INT, square INT" def reader(self, schema): return CounterReader(self.options) class CounterReader(DataSourceReader): def __init__(self, options): self.limit = int(options.get("limit", 3)) def read(self, partition): for i in range(1, self.limit + 1): yield (i, i * i) spark.dataSource.register(CounterDataSource) spark.read.format("counter").option("limit", 4).load().show() # n 1..4, square 1, 4, 9, 16 from pyspark.sql.functions import udtf @udtf(returnType="word: string, length: int") class SplitWords: def eval(self, text: str): for w in text.split(): yield (w, len(w)) spark.udtf.register("split_words", SplitWords) spark.sql("SELECT * FROM split_words('spark four point zero')").show() # spark 5, four 4, point 5, zero 4 When it fits, and when it doesn’t It fits when the source is an API or a custom file format and a few lines of Python will do. If a JVM connector already exists, or the source has to be as fast as possible, use that instead. The usual stumble is running without PyArrow. Image 18: Two classes and one registration call make the source readable by name. 9. GROUP BY on maps and DESCRIBE … AS JSON Since: 4.0.0 · Area: SQL · Source: SPARK-47430, SPARK-50541 Lineage: new in 4.0. Two small gaps closed together. GROUP BY now accepts a MAP column (SPARK-47430), and DESCRIBE ... AS JSON returns a table’s description as a JSON document a program can read (SPARK-50541). Grouping by a map was an error before. Comparing two maps with = still isn’t allowed in 4.0: a MAP can be a grouping key, and a join on one fails with [DATATYPE_MISMATCH.INVALID_ORDERING_TYPE]. Before Spark 4.0 To group by a map you had to turn it into something sortable, usually a JSON string. Runnable file: 22_group_by_map_before.sql. SELECT to_json(m) AS m, count(*) AS n FROM VALUES (map('k', 1)), (map('k', 1)), (map('k', 2)) AS t(m) GROUP BY to_json(m) ORDER BY n; -- {"k":2} 1, {"k":1} 2 Image 19: The grouping key stays a map instead of turning into a string. With Spark 4.0: sample code Runnable file: 10_group_by_map_describe_json.sql. SELECT m, count(*) AS n FROM VALUES (map('k', 1)), (map('k', 1)), (map('k', 2)) AS t(m) GROUP BY m ORDER BY n; -- {k -> 2} 1, {k -> 1} 2 CREATE TABLE people (id INT, name STRING) USING parquet; DESCRIBE EXTENDED people AS JSON; -- one JSON document When it fits, and when it doesn’t Group by a map when the map is the identity of the row, a set of labels for example. For a join, extract the keys you need and compare those. DESCRIBE ... AS JSON is for tooling that inspects table metadata; for reading by eye, plain DESCRIBE is easier. Image 20: Maps group as maps, and a table describes itself as JSON. 10. transformWithState and the state data source Since: 4.0.0 · Area: Streaming · Source: SPARK-46815, SPARK-45511 Lineage: applyInPandasWithState and flatMapGroupsWithState came before; transformWithState is the new API. Structured Streaming remembers things per key between micro-batches, a running count for example. That memory is called state. transformWithState (SPARK-46815) lets you write the logic yourself as a stateful processor: a class with an init method that declares typed state variables, a handleInputRows method that receives the rows for one key, and a close method. It exists in Scala, Java and Python, where the Python form is transformWithStateInPandas. The state data source (SPARK-45511) reads that state back as a table with spark.read.format("statestore"), so you can query what a stream remembers instead of guessing. Two things have to be set up first, and each one fails with its own error if it isn’t. A processor’s state variables are separate column families, which only the RocksDB state store supports, so the default provider fails with UNSUPPORTED_FEATURE.STATE_STORE_MULTIPLE_COLUMN_FAMILIES. And the Python runner needs protobuf and the gRPC packages; without them the query fails with STREAMING_PYTHON_RUNNER_INITIALIZATION_FAILURE. With Spark 4.0: sample code Runnable file: 12_transform_with_state.py. # needs RocksDBStateStoreProvider as the state store, and pip install protobuf grpcio class CountProcessor(StatefulProcessor): def init(self, handle): schema = StructType([StructField("value", IntegerType())]) self.count = handle.getValueState("count", schema) def handleInputRows(self, key, rows, timerValues): total = self.count.get()[0] if self.count.exists() else 0 for pdf in rows: total += len(pdf) self.count.update((total,)) yield pd.DataFrame({"id": [key[0]], "count": [total]}) def close(self): pass counts = stream.groupBy("id").transformWithStateInPandas(statefulProcessor=CountProcessor(), outputStructType="id STRING, count INT", outputMode="Update", timeMode="None") state = spark.read.format("statestore").option("stateVarName", "count").load(checkpoint) # [('0', 78), ('1', 78), ('2', 78)] from both the output and the state data source The rate source produced the keys 0, 1 and 2, and after 40 seconds each key held 78, in the output and in the state data source alike. The number depends on how long the query runs. Reading state before any batch has committed fails with STDS_COMMITTED_BATCH_UNAVAILABLE. When it fits, and when it doesn’t Use it when a stream needs custom per-key logic, such as running counts, sessions or timers, and you want to be able to look at the state. A plain groupBy(...).count() does the job when all you need is a count, and then you can skip all of this setup. There’s no before-and-after pair for this one, because the older state APIs work differently enough that the code doesn’t translate line by line. Image 21: The same per-key counts come out of the query and out of the state data source. Smaller additions worth knowing Feature What it does Needs Named and unnamed parameter markers (SPARK-41666) spark.sql("SELECT :a + :b", args={...}) and ? with a list; values stay out of the SQL text Nothing Polymorphic Python UDTFs analyze() decides the output schema from the arguments Nothing EXECUTE IMMEDIATE (SPARK-46246) Runs a SQL string with bound parameters Nothing Lightweight Python client and spark.api.mode The pyspark-client package, about 1.5 MB, and a setting to turn Spark Connect on Nothing ML on Spark Connect pyspark.ml over a Connect server A Connect server Structured JSON logging (SPARK-47240) Machine-readable driver and executor logs, enabled with spark.log.structuredLogging.enabled The setting Spark Kubernetes operator (SPARK-45923) Run Spark applications as Kubernetes custom resources A Kubernetes cluster PySpark plotting API (SPARK-49530) df.plot.bar(x="k", y="v") returns a Plotly figure plotly installed Unified PySpark UDF profiling One profiler for Python UDFs Nothing Smaller additions in code Parameter markers and a polymorphic UDTF. Runnable file: 13_pyspark_extras.py. spark.sql("SELECT :a + :b AS s", args={"a": 1, "b": 2}) # 3, named, bound from a dictionary spark.sql("SELECT ? + ? AS s", args=[1, 2]) # 3, unnamed, bound from a list spark.sql("SELECT :s AS s", args={"s": "x'; DROP TABLE t; --"}) # comes back as a plain string @udtf class Echo: @staticmethod def analyze(a: AnalyzeArgument) -> AnalyzeResult: return AnalyzeResult(StructType().add("c1", a.dataType)) def eval(self, a): yield (a,) spark.udtf.register("echo", Echo) spark.sql("SELECT * FROM echo(5)") # c1 int spark.sql("SELECT * FROM echo('x')") # c1 string EXECUTE IMMEDIATE. Runnable file: 08_execute_immediate.sql. EXECUTE IMMEDIATE 'SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE amount > ?' USING 8; -- 3 In 4.0 a parameter marker stands where a literal value would, so it can’t replace a table name. Version lineage Most of these are new in 4.0. The 3.5 column is what you had before. Feature 3.5 4.0 ANSI mode A setting, off by default On by default (SPARK-44444) Semi-structured data JSON strings and get_json_object VARIANT (SPARK-45827) SQL syntax SELECT ... FROM only Pipe syntax (SPARK-49555) Reusable logic Python and Scala UDFs SQL UDFs and session variables (SPARK-46057, SPARK-42849) Strings Binary comparison Collation (SPARK-46830) XML An external package A built-in source and functions (SPARK-44265) Python extensibility Python UDTFs (SPARK-43797) Data Source API and polymorphic UDTFs (SPARK-44076) Streaming state applyInPandasWithState, flatMapGroupsWithState transformWithState, state data source (SPARK-46815, SPARK-45511) Platform Scala 2.12 and 2.13, Java 8, 11 and 17 Scala 2.13 and Java 17 or 21 (SPARK-45314, SPARK-45315) Settings and costs Defaults the 4.0 release notes list as changed. Setting Default in 4.0 Source spark.sql.ansi.enabled true SPARK-44444 spark.eventLog.rolling.enabled true SPARK-45771 spark.ui.prometheus.enabled true SPARK-46886 spark.shuffle.service.db.backend ROCKSDB SPARK-45351 Feature Cost to plan for ANSI mode The change most likely to turn a green pipeline red. Test your real data before the upgrade Python data source and UDTFs PyArrow must be installed on every node that runs a Python worker transformWithState The RocksDB state store, and protobuf and gRPC packages for the Python form Scala 2.13 and Java 17 Every jar the jobs depend on needs a Scala 2.13 build When these features bite These are the errors you’re most likely to hit, with the text Spark prints so you can search for it. Each one has its own anchor, so you can link straight to it. [UNSUPPORTED_FEATURE.STATE_STORE_MULTIPLE_COLUMN_FAMILIES]. transformWithState stores each state variable as its own column family, and the default HDFS-backed state store doesn’t support that. Fix: Set spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.providerClass to the RocksDB provider. [STREAMING_PYTHON_RUNNER_INITIALIZATION_FAILURE] with ImportError: cannot import name 'descriptor' from 'google.protobuf'. The Python runner for transformWithStateInPandas needs protobuf and the gRPC packages, which the official image lacks. Fix: pip install protobuf grpcio grpcio-status googleapis-common-protos. [STDS_COMMITTED_BATCH_UNAVAILABLE]. The state data source was read before the query committed a batch. Fix: Let the query commit at least one micro-batch before you read its checkpoint. [CAST_INVALID_INPUT], [DIVIDE_BY_ZERO]. ANSI mode is on by default, so work that silently produced NULL now stops. Fix: Use try_cast and try_divide where NULL was the intended answer, or set spark.sql.ansi.enabled=false while you fix the data. ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pyarrow' from the Python data source worker. The official image has no PyArrow. Fix: Install pyarrow and pandas. [DATATYPE_MISMATCH.INVALID_ORDERING_TYPE] on map(...) = map(...). A MAP can be a grouping key in 4.0, but two maps can’t be compared with =. Fix: Group on the map; don’t join on it. Upgrade checklist: what can break For most teams the move from 3.x is more than a version bump: Scala, Java, ANSI and a long list of defaults change. Work through this on a staging copy of your heaviest job first. 1. Runtime and dependencies Requirement 4.0 value Source Java 17 or 21; JDK 8 and 11 are dropped Spark 4.0.5 overview, SPARK-45315 Scala 2.13 only; Scala 2.12 is dropped SPARK-45314 Python 3.9 or newer requires_python of pyspark==4.0.5 on PyPI pandas, PyArrow, NumPy (pyspark[sql]) 2.0.0, 11.0.0 and 1.21 or newer requires_dist on PyPI pyspark[connect] extras grpcio and grpcio-status 1.67.0 or newer requires_dist on PyPI Kafka connector spark-sql-kafka-0-10_2.13:4.0.5 is published Maven Central 2. Check every connector jar before you upgrade Connector runtimes are built per Spark minor version and per Scala version, so a jar built for Spark 3.5 and Scala 2.12 won’t load. List the artifacts from your spark.jars.packages and ask Maven Central whether each has a 4.0.5 build, so you find a missing one before the cluster does. Runnable file: 23_check_maven_artifacts.py. import urllib.request # group, artifact: edit to match your spark.jars.packages ARTIFACTS = [ ("org.apache.spark", "spark-sql-kafka-0-10_2.13"), ("org.apache.spark", "spark-avro_2.13"), ] SPARK = "4.0.5" for group, artifact in ARTIFACTS: base = f"https://repo1.maven.org/maven2/{group.replace('.', '/')}/{artifact}" try: urllib.request.urlopen(f"{base}/{SPARK}/{artifact}-{SPARK}.pom", timeout=10) print(f"OK {artifact}:{SPARK}") except Exception: print(f"MISSING {artifact} -> no {SPARK} build published") The output: OK spark-sql-kafka-0-10_2.13:4.0.5 OK spark-avro_2.13:4.0.5 For third-party connectors, the artifact name carries both the Scala and the Spark version, so use the name the project documents for Spark 4.0. A MISSING line means keep those jobs on their current Spark version. 3. Behaviour changes to test These come from the official SQL and PySpark migration guides and the release notes, which list many more. Change What to do Source Scala 2.13 and JDK 17 are the baseline; Scala 2.12 and JDK 8 and 11 are gone Rebuild every jar for Scala 2.13 SPARK-45314, SPARK-45315 ANSI mode is on by default Test your data; use try_*; spark.sql.ansi.enabled=false restores NULL SPARK-44444 CREATE TABLE without USING uses spark.sql.sources.default, not Hive spark.sql.legacy.createHiveTableByDefault=true SQL migration guide ORC default compression is zstd, not snappy spark.sql.orc.compression.codec=snappy SQL migration guide Inner CTEs take precedence (ctePrecedencePolicy is CORRECTED) spark.sql.legacy.ctePrecedencePolicy=EXCEPTION or LEGACY SQL migration guide Timestamp parse failures raise CANNOT_PARSE_TIMESTAMP in ANSI mode, NULL otherwise spark.sql.legacy.timeParserPolicy=EXCEPTION SQL migration guide ! is no longer accepted as NOT in expr ! IN (...) and similar spark.sql.legacy.bangEqualsNot=true, or write NOT SQL migration guide JDBC type mappings changed for Postgres, MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server and DB2 Per-database spark.sql.legacy.*Mapping.enabled settings, listed in the guide SQL migration guide Hive metastore versions before 2.0.0 are unsupported Upgrade the metastore SQL migration guide Python 3.8 dropped; pandas 2.0.0, NumPy 1.21 and PyArrow 11.0.0 are the minimums Upgrade the Python environment SPARK-47993, SPARK-50657 Many pandas API on Spark removals (iteritems, append, mad, Int64Index) and compute.ops_on_diff_frames on by default Run your pandas-on-Spark code first PySpark migration guide from pyspark.sql.functions import * no longer exports DataFrame, Column or StructType Import them from pyspark.sql or pyspark.sql.types PySpark migration guide A map column’s schema is inferred from all key-value pairs, not the first spark.sql.pyspark.legacy.inferMapTypeFromFirstPair.enabled=true PySpark migration guide spark.eventLog.rolling.enabled, spark.ui.prometheus.enabled and a RocksDB shuffle-service store are on by default Recheck log and metrics setups SPARK-45771, SPARK-46886, SPARK-45351 4. Roll out in this order Dependencies first. Rebuild your jars for Scala 2.13 and run the connector script above. Keep any job whose connector is missing where it is. Python. Move to a supported Python with PyArrow 11.0.0 or newer, and test the pandas-on-Spark changes. Turn ANSI off first, then on. Run the batch job on 4.0 with spark.sql.ansi.enabled=false to separate the upgrade from the data problems, then turn it on and fix what it finds. Batch jobs. Compare outputs and runtimes against the old cluster. Streaming jobs last. Restart a copy of each job from a copy of its existing checkpoint in staging first, and keep the old checkpoint and the old Spark version until that run passes. 5. Common mistakes Leaving ANSI untested. It’s the most common reason a job that worked on 3.x fails on 4.0. Forgetting rowTag. The XML reader needs it. Running transformWithState on the default state store. Switch to RocksDB first. Running the Python data source without PyArrow. The official image doesn’t have it. Comparing maps with =. Group by a map, don’t join on one. Known limitations in this release ANSI mode. Invalid casts and divide by zero are the commonly hit cases; other ANSI behaviours, such as overflow, change too. XML. The reader needs a rowTag, and the inferred field order is alphabetical. Python data source and UDTFs. PyArrow has to be installed on every node that runs a Python worker. transformWithState. The RocksDB state store is required, and the counts in the sample depend on how long the query ran. Maps. A MAP can be a grouping key, but two maps can’t be compared with =. Cheat sheet Image 22: The syntax of each feature and what has to be on first. Download the cheat sheet as a PNG. Frequently Asked Questions What is new in Apache Spark 4.0? Spark 4.0.0, released on 23 May 2025, makes Scala 2.13 and Java 17 the baseline, turns ANSI mode on by default, and adds VARIANT, SQL pipe syntax, SQL UDFs, session variables, string collation, a built-in XML source, the Python Data Source API and transformWithState. Why did my job start failing with CAST_INVALID_INPUT after upgrading? ANSI mode is on by default in 4.0, so a bad cast raises where it used to return NULL. Use try_cast, or set spark.sql.ansi.enabled=false while you fix the data. Which Scala and Java versions does Spark 4.0 need? Scala 2.13 and Java 17. Scala 2.12 and JDK 8 and 11 are no longer supported, so jars need a Scala 2.13 build. What Python version does Spark 4.0 need? Python 3.9 or newer, with pandas 2.0.0, PyArrow 11.0.0 and NumPy 1.21 as the minimums for the sql extra. How do I read XML in Spark 4.0? Use spark.read.format("xml").option("rowTag", "person").load(path) for files, or from_xml for XML held in a string column. No external package is needed. Why does my Python data source fail with No module named 'pyarrow'? The data source worker moves rows through Arrow. The official image doesn’t ship PyArrow, so pip install pyarrow pandas, or use pip install "pyspark[sql]". Why does transformWithState fail on the default state store? Each state variable is a separate column family, which only RocksDB supports. Set spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.providerClass to the RocksDB provider. Can I group by a map column? Yes, in 4.0. Comparing two maps with = is still an error, so group on the map and don’t join on it. Which Spark 4.0 release should I use? 4.0.5 is the latest 4.0 release. Fixes land in the patch releases, so start there. Is it safe to turn ANSI mode off? It’s a valid stopgap, and spark.sql.ansi.enabled=false restores the old behaviour. Treat it as a way to separate the upgrade from your data problems, not as the place to stay. Summary Spark 4.0 changes the baseline and the defaults, and adds the SQL features that were missing. ANSI mode makes bad data visible, VARIANT, UDFs, variables, collation and pipe syntax make SQL more capable, and the XML source and Python Data Source API reduce the connectors you need to build. A few things need setup, PyArrow or the RocksDB state store, so check those before you plan around them. If you only test one thing before upgrading, make it ANSI mode against your real data. It’s the change that decides whether the rest of the move is smooth. Further reading Spark 4.0.0 release notes, the source of the ticket numbers above SQL pipe syntax in the SQL reference ANSI compliance in the SQL reference The Spark versioning policy Spark release history for what was removed and when What’s new in Apache Spark 4.1 for the release after this one Spark 4.x features by release for all the releases side by side Trademarks Apache Spark, Apache Kafka, Apache Parquet, Apache Arrow and Apache are either registered trademarks or trademarks of The Apache Software Foundation in the United States and other countries. The Apache Software Foundation does not endorse this post.

entry.title: Six URL rewrites that turn any GitHub repository into an editor, a prompt, a diagram or an MCP server

link.title: Six URL rewrites that turn any GitHub repository into an editor, a prompt, a diagram or an MCP server

entry.content:
• Why read a repository without cloning it
    • The test repository
  • What the URL rewrite actually does
    • Three jobs, three places the work happens
    • The trade-off all six share
  • Hands-on demo: each tool, step by step, on a real repository
    • Tool 1: github1s, a read-only VS Code in the tab
    • Tool 2: GitIngest, the whole repository as one prompt
    • Tool 3: GitDiagram, an architecture diagram from the file tree
    • Tool 4: GitMCP, the repository as a tool your assistant can call
    • Tool 5: GitHubBox, a running dev environment, for the right repo
    • Tool 6: DeepWiki, a generated wiki, if someone has indexed it
  • Real-world scenarios and production failures
    • Failure 1: the prompt is bigger than the model can use
    • Failure 2: the diagram says something the repository does not
    • Failure 3: the same URLs refuse a script
    • Failure 4: a stale snapshot treated as current
    • Failure 5: what you paste and what you sign up for
    • Failure 6: wrong tool for the repository
  • Optimisation, tuning knobs and best practices
    • Pick the tool by the question, not by the novelty
    • A pipeline that uses three of them
    • Scope before you paste
    • Check what you are about to send
    • Prompt template for a dump
    • Cost and trade-offs against a local clone
  • Key takeaways
  • References
  • Trademarks

TL;DR

  • Six sites work by rewriting the host or the path of a GitHub URL. No install, no clone, and for public repositories no sign-in.
  • They split into three jobs: read a repo (github1s), feed a repo to an LLM (GitIngest, GitMCP), and understand a repo (GitDiagram, DeepWiki). GitHubBox is the odd one out: it runs a repo, and only helps if the repo is a JavaScript project.
  • Every screenshot in this post comes from one real repository, rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments: 280 text files, Scala and Java, Maven build. That choice exposes the limits as well as the wins.
  • Two of the tools did not work for this repo, and the post says so and shows why.

Why read a repository without cloning it

A pull request link, a Stack Overflow answer or a colleague’s message lands you in a repository you have never seen. The default move is git clone, then an IDE import, then a Maven or sbt dependency download, all to answer a question like “where does this job write its output?”. For a repository you will not touch again, that is minutes of setup for a thirty-second question.

A family of small sites removes the setup by taking the GitHub URL itself as input. You change github.com to another host, or put another host in front of the path, and the page you land on has done the work: an editor with search, a single text file ready to paste into a chat, a diagram, or a server your AI assistant can query.

This post runs each of them, in order, on the same repository so the outputs are comparable. It is a tutorial first: each tool has numbered steps and a screenshot taken during the run. It also records where each tool stops, because “works on any repo” is only true of some of them.

The test repository

All runs use rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments. It is a good subject because it is awkward in the ways real repositories are:

Property Value Why it matters
Files 280 text files analysed by GitIngest Large enough that a naive dump is cropped
Layout 34 top-level folders, 32 of them Maven modules (each has a pom.xml), one per Spark integration A diagram has to summarise, not list
Languages Scala 153,704 bytes, Java 41,228, Shell 23,514, Python 5,074 (GitHub languages API) Not JavaScript, which matters for GitHubBox
History 102 commits, one branch, last commit eaf9e23 Small enough to read, old enough to be unmaintained

What the URL rewrite actually does

None of these sites is magic. Each one is a web application that receives owner/repo in the URL, fetches the repository from GitHub on the server side (or, for github1s, in your browser), and renders a different view of it. The rewrite is the cheapest possible interface: you already have the GitHub URL, so the only thing you type is the part that changes.

  https://github.com/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments
        |
        |  swap the host, keep owner/repo
        v
  github1s.com   /rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments   -> VS Code in the browser
  gitingest.com  /rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments   -> one text file for an LLM
  gitdiagram.com /rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments   -> architecture diagram
  gitmcp.io      /rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments   -> MCP server URL
  githubbox.com  /rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments   -> redirects to CodeSandbox
  deepwiki.com   /rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments   -> generated wiki, if indexed

All six take the same two path segments. Only the host differs, so the habit to build is: open the repository on GitHub, then retype the host.

Three jobs, three places the work happens

The tools differ less in what they show than in where the computation runs and what they cost you.

Tool Job Where the work runs What you get Needs sign-in
github1s Read and search Your browser, which loads a VS Code web build A read-only VS Code workbench No
GitIngest Feed an LLM Server One text file: summary, tree, file contents No
GitMCP Feed an LLM, live Server, over MCP A URL your assistant calls as tools No
GitDiagram Understand Server, using an LLM A Mermaid diagram of the architecture No
DeepWiki Understand Server, using an LLM A wiki, after an indexing job Email to index
GitHubBox Run CodeSandbox A cloud dev environment Not to open

“Needs sign-in” is for a public repository, as observed in this run. Private repositories need tokens or accounts on most of these, and none was tried here.

The trade-off all six share

Each tool trades privacy and completeness for speed. The server-side ones receive the repository name, and GitHubBox, GitIngest and GitDiagram each run on someone else’s infrastructure, so none of them belongs anywhere near a private repository you have not cleared. The model-backed ones (GitDiagram, DeepWiki) also summarise: they read a slice of the repository, which the sections below quantify (GitDiagram reported reading 40 source files out of 280).

The alternative is the tool you already have: git clone --depth 1, then tree, rg and your IDE. It is complete, private and offline, and it costs the clone plus the import. The six tools win on the first minute and lose on everything after it.

Hands-on demo: each tool, step by step, on a real repository

Every step below was run on 12 November 2026 in Chrome against the repository above, signed in to nothing but GitHub. The screenshots are from those runs, unedited apart from file size. Each tool section ends with what it did not do, because that is the part the landing pages leave out.

Tool 1: github1s, a read-only VS Code in the tab

What it is for. Browsing and searching code with a real editor’s tree, tabs and search panel, without cloning. It is the right first move when you want to read, not run.

Steps

  1. Open the repository on GitHub: https://github.com/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments.
  2. Edit the host in the address bar: replace github.com with github1s.com. The full URL is https://github1s.com/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments.
  3. Wait for the workbench to load. It opens the README as a preview tab and the whole folder tree in the Explorer. The status bar shows master, the branch the URL resolved to.

  1. To land on a file directly, keep the whole GitHub path and change only the host. This opens the Delta Lake example:
https://github1s.com/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments/blob/master/spark-delta-lake-integration/src/main/scala/com/ranga/spark/delta/lake/SparkDeltaLakeIntegrationApp.scala

  1. Search across the repository. Click the magnifier in the activity bar, or press Cmd+Shift+F on macOS (Ctrl+Shift+F elsewhere), and type format("delta"). The panel reported 2 results in 1 file, and both matches are highlighted in the open editor.

Where it stops

  • No syntax highlighting for Scala. The status bar showed Plain Text for the .scala file. Navigation and search work; colour does not.
  • Read-only. The Search view has a Replace box, but this is a viewer for a public repository. There is nothing to run, build or debug.
  • A “Leave site?” prompt. After I used Search, Chrome asked for confirmation before navigating away from the page. It is a browser prompt from the editor page, not data loss, because nothing can be saved.

Tool 2: GitIngest, the whole repository as one prompt

What it is for. Pasting a repository into an LLM chat. It produces a summary, a directory tree and the file contents as a single text document.

Steps

  1. Open https://gitingest.com/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments. The path is the same owner/repo, so the page starts processing immediately.
  2. Wait for the spinner. This run took under half a minute for 280 files.
  3. Read the Summary panel. For this repository it reported:
Repository: rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments
Commit: eaf9e23df97e7f3dbe720223b027fb24352f3f5f
Files analyzed: 280

Estimated tokens: 173.5k

  1. Use the controls above the result before you ingest, not after. The form has an Exclude (or Include) pattern box such as *.md, src/, an Include files under slider that defaults to 50 kB, and a Private Repository checkbox. Typing *.xml, *.sh, *.md, *.properties into the Exclude box and clicking Ingest again took the result from 280 files and 173.5k estimated tokens to 151 files and 64.1k tokens, with the same commit.

  1. Click Copy all to put the document on the clipboard, or Download to save it as a file. Paste it into a chat with the question you actually have, for example “Which modules write to Kafka and which read from it?”

Where it stops

  • The on-page view is cropped. The panel begins with (Files content cropped to 300k characters, download full ingest to see more). The 173.5k-token estimate is for the whole repository, so only Download gives you everything.
  • 173.5k tokens does not fit everywhere. It is a large prompt even for long-context models. Exclude patterns are not optional for a repository this size.
  • A snapshot, not a live view. The summary pins commit eaf9e23. A later push is not in the document you copied.

Tool 3: GitDiagram, an architecture diagram from the file tree

What it is for. The first ninety seconds with an unfamiliar repository: what are the parts and how do they connect.

Steps

  1. Open https://gitdiagram.com/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments.
  2. Watch the progress panel. It shows Understanding the architecture with a timer and an Info line, 40 source files read. The diagram appeared after roughly half a minute.
  3. The first render fits the whole diagram into the page. For this repository it is too wide to read:

  1. Click Enable zoom. The diagram becomes pannable and zoomable (the first view opened at 467%), with -, + and FIT controls. Scroll and drag to read a cluster:

  1. The toolbar also has Export and Regenerate. For use in your own notes, add .md to the URL:
https://gitdiagram.com/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments.md

That returned 200 with text/markdown, about 15 KB, containing an Overview, the diagram as a Mermaid block, a Components list with links to source files, and Connections. It is built for pasting into an agent’s context instead of screenshotting the page.

Where it stops

  • It reads a sample. Forty files out of 280. Its own markdown says it is generated “from its file tree, README and a sample of source files” and that it “is an AI-made overview: check details against the source.”
  • It invents hubs. The top node, Example runner, fans out to every cluster. This repository is a set of independent examples, and the generated overview itself says each is “independently initiated”. The hub is the model’s way to draw a tree, not a program in the repo. Read diagrams like this as a table of contents, not a call graph.
  • Wide repositories shrink. Thirty-two sibling modules produce a diagram that only works zoomed. A repository with a deeper structure would read better than a flat monorepo of samples.

Tool 4: GitMCP, the repository as a tool your assistant can call

What it is for. Instead of pasting a snapshot, give an AI assistant a URL that it queries on demand, so it reads current files rather than a stale dump.

Steps

  1. Open https://gitmcp.io/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments. The page is a setup guide titled GitMCP Documentation Server, with the server URL:
https://gitmcp.io/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments
  1. Pick your client from the tabs: Cursor, Claude Desktop, Windsurf, VSCode, Cline, Highlight AI, Augment Code or Msty AI. For Cursor, add this to ~/.cursor/mcp.json:
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "ranga_spark_experiments Docs": {
      "url": "https://gitmcp.io/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments"
    }
  }
}

  1. For Claude Desktop the page gives a different shape, because that client starts a local process and bridges to the remote server with mcp-remote. Add this to claude_desktop_config.json:
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "ranga_spark_experiments Docs": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": [
        "mcp-remote",
        "https://gitmcp.io/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments"
      ]
    }
  }
}

  1. Restart the client and ask a question that needs the repository, such as “In ranga_spark_experiments, how does the graceful shutdown example stop a streaming job?”

Where it stops

  • Not run end to end in this post. The configuration above is exactly what the page shows. I did not connect an assistant to the server or list its tools, so what the assistant does with the URL is not claimed here.
  • Claude Desktop needs Node. npx mcp-remote means a local Node.js install, which cancels some of the “no install” appeal for that client.
  • Editing the config file is the install. A remote MCP URL means the assistant sends your questions, and what it fetches, to a third-party server.

Tool 5: GitHubBox, a running dev environment, for the right repo

What it is for. Opening a repository as an editable, runnable project in CodeSandbox, which suits JavaScript and Node projects.

Steps

  1. Open https://githubbox.com/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments.
  2. It redirects to https://codesandbox.io/p/sandbox/github/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments, shows “Fetching details…”, then opens the editor. It opened without a sign-in, with a Sign In button still available.

Where it stops, and this one stopped. The preview pane is blank. The template label reads nodebox, a Node runtime in the browser, and this repository is Scala and Java built with Maven: no package.json, nothing for a Node sandbox to start. It is a useful negative result. GitHubBox is for JavaScript repositories, and nothing in this post is evidence that it works for anything else. I did not test it on a Node repository.

Tool 6: DeepWiki, a generated wiki, if someone has indexed it

What it is for. An LLM-written wiki of a repository, with pages by topic.

Steps

  1. Open https://deepwiki.com/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments.
  2. For this repository the page showed Repository Not Indexed: “This repository hasn’t been indexed yet”, with the estimate “Indexing typically takes 2-10 minutes”.

  1. Indexing requires an email to notify (required) and a click on Index Repository. I stopped here. Submitting someone’s email address to a third-party service is not part of a read-only demonstration, so the wiki itself is not covered in this post.

Where it stops. It does not work on first visit for a repository nobody has indexed, and the index step has a cost in personal data. For well-known projects that are already indexed it is the lowest-effort tool of the six, but I have not shown that here.

Real-world scenarios and production failures

These tools are for reading, so “production failure” here means the moment a workflow built on one of them gives a wrong answer or quietly stops working. Each case below was observed in this run unless it says otherwise.

Failure 1: the prompt is bigger than the model can use

The GitIngest summary for the unfiltered repository says Estimated tokens: 173.5k. Pasting that into a chat either fails the length limit or, worse, fits and leaves little room for the answer. The page does not stop you. It crops its own preview to 300k characters and leaves the decision with you.

The fix is to cut before copying, not after. Excluding build files, shell scripts, Markdown and properties files removed 129 of 280 files and cut the estimate from 173.5k to 64.1k tokens at the same commit. Mind what you removed: that exclude list also drops the pom.xml files, so a question about dependencies now has no evidence to read.

Run Files Estimated tokens
Defaults (50 kB file limit) 280 173.5k
Exclude *.xml, *.sh, *.md, *.properties 151 64.1k

Failure 2: the diagram says something the repository does not

GitDiagram’s top node is Example runner, with a labelled runs edge to every cluster. Read at face value it says one entry point launches all the examples. The same tool’s text overview says the opposite: “Each example is independently initiated.” Both statements came out of one generation.

The root cause is structural. A diagram needs a root, a flat collection of 32 independent modules does not have one, and the model supplies a hub. The tool also states it read 40 files, so any behaviour that lives in the other 240 is a guess from names. Treat the diagram as an index of where to look, then confirm in the source (github1s is the quickest way to do that).

Failure 3: the same URLs refuse a script

All of these loaded in the browser. Requested from a shell with curl, the same hosts answered differently:

URL (path /rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments) Browser curl status
githubbox.com Redirected to CodeSandbox and opened 403
deepwiki.com “Repository Not Indexed” page 429
uithub.com Not opened in the browser 401
gitmcp.io Setup page 200
gitingest.com Result page 200
gitdiagram.com Result page 200

The page-level 200 for GitIngest, GitDiagram and GitMCP only proves that a page was served. I did not trace how each one fetches its results, so a bare curl of the page is not shown here to be a way to automate them. If you want repeatable output in CI, use the repository’s own tooling: git clone --depth 1 and a local packer, not these sites. The one exception observed is GitDiagram’s .md endpoint, which returned the generated text over plain curl with a 200.

Failure 4: a stale snapshot treated as current

GitIngest pins the commit in its summary (eaf9e23...). Anything pushed after that is not in your document, and nothing in the pasted text tells the model so. If you are asking an assistant about a fast-moving repository, put the commit hash into the prompt and refresh the dump before a long session. This repository last changed in December 2023, so staleness did not bite here, and I did not test a repository that changes daily.

Failure 5: what you paste and what you sign up for

  • Everything included is sent to the model. GitIngest includes every file under the size limit that your pattern does not exclude. If a repository has a committed credential in a config file, it is in the dump. Scan or exclude before copying. This is a general risk with any dump tool, not something I found in this repository.
  • Private repositories. GitIngest has a Private Repository checkbox and GitDiagram has API Key and Private Repos entries in its header. I did not test either, and handing a private repository’s code to a free third-party service is a decision for your security team, not a URL trick.
  • DeepWiki asks for an email. To index a repository you must give an address. The post stopped there on purpose.
  • Ads and sponsors. GitIngest shows Carbon ads and GitDiagram a sponsor banner. This is how free tools pay for the servers that read your repository, and a reason to keep them off pages with sensitive context.

Failure 6: wrong tool for the repository

GitHubBox is the clean example. For this Scala and Java repository, the editor opened and the preview was empty, which looks like an error on your side, not a mismatch. The test before you open any of these tools is one question about the repository: what is its main language, and what do I want out of it?

If the repository is Reach for Skip
JavaScript or Node, and you want to run it GitHubBox Nothing, but expect to wait for installs
Any language, and you want to read it github1s GitHubBox
Any language, and you want to ask an LLM GitIngest for a one-off, GitMCP for repeated use Pasting the unfiltered dump
Large, unfamiliar, and you want the shape GitDiagram, then verify in github1s Trusting the hub node
Popular open source project DeepWiki, if already indexed Indexing someone else’s repo with your email

Optimisation, tuning knobs and best practices

The tools have few settings, so the tuning is mostly about what you decide before you open them and what you do with the output afterwards.

Pick the tool by the question, not by the novelty

  What do you want to know?
        |
        +-- "Where is X, and how is it written?" ---------> github1s
        |                                                    (read, search)
        +-- "What are the parts and how do they connect?" -> GitDiagram
        |                                                    (then verify in github1s)
        +-- "Answer questions about it, once" ------------> GitIngest
        |                                                    (scope with excludes first)
        +-- "Answer questions about it, repeatedly" ------> GitMCP
        |                                                    (the assistant fetches on demand)
        +-- "Does it run?" (Node/JS only) ----------------> GitHubBox
        +-- "A wiki for a well-known project" ------------> DeepWiki
                                                             (only if already indexed)

Walk the diagram top to bottom. The first two branches need no AI at all for the answer: github1s is plain browsing. The AI-backed branches (GitIngest, GitMCP, GitDiagram, DeepWiki) are where you should check the result.

A pipeline that uses three of them

For an unfamiliar repository, in this order:

  1. GitDiagram for the shape. Open the .md version if you want to paste the overview and component list into your notes. Write down the two or three clusters that matter to you.
  2. github1s to confirm. Open one file from each cluster and read it. This is where the Example runner hub gets caught.
  3. GitIngest, scoped for the deep question. Exclude everything outside the clusters you picked, so the token count matches the question.
  4. GitMCP if you will keep asking. A configured MCP URL beats re-pasting a dump every session, and does not go stale the way a pinned dump does. (Configuration shown above; not exercised end to end in this post.)

Scope before you paste

GitIngest’s controls are the only real tuning surface in the set.

Control Default seen What it does Use it when
Exclude / Include pattern empty Glob patterns, comma separated, e.g. *.md, src/ Always, for anything over a few dozen files
Include files under 50 kB Skips larger files Generated or data files dominate
Private Repository off Checkbox for private repositories Not tested here

Measured on this repository, one exclude list changed the result like this:

Exclude list Files Estimated tokens
None 280 173.5k
*.xml, *.sh, *.md, *.properties 151 64.1k

Patterns worth trying, as starting points and not measured here: exclude test folders when the question is about production code, exclude *.json and *.csv for data-heavy repositories, and use Include mode to keep only one module’s directory. Verify the file count after each change, because a pattern that matches more than you meant removes the evidence for your question.

Check what you are about to send

Before pasting a dump anywhere, run two local commands on a shallow clone. They cost almost nothing and they are the check the web tools do not give you:

git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments
cd ranga_spark_experiments
git ls-files | wc -l
grep -rIn --exclude-dir=.git -E 'AKIA|password *=|secret' .

On this repository that printed 313 tracked files, and the grep produced a handful of hits that were all configuration key names and placeholders: Hadoop fs.s3a.secret.key settings that read the value from a variable, a usage string with the literal arguments ranga_aws_access_key ranga_aws_secret_key, and a spark.datasource.hive.warehouse.password=hive line in a run script. No real credential. That outcome is the point of the exercise: a pattern search finds names, so a person has to triage it, and it is quicker to do that on a terminal than after the text is in a chat.

The file counts differ by tool and the post did not reconcile them: git ls-files says 313, GitIngest analysed 280, and 151 after excludes. Different tools count binary files, ignored files and size limits differently. Compare counts within a tool, not across tools.

Prompt template for a dump

A pasted repository answers better when the prompt says what the text is.

Below is a snapshot of github.com/<owner>/<repo> at commit <sha>,
filtered to <what you kept>. Answer only from this text. If the answer is
not in it, say which file you would need. Quote file paths.

Question: <your question>

The commit hash comes from the Summary panel (eaf9e23... here). It tells the assistant, and your future self, which snapshot the answer is about. The “which file you would need” line is the cheap guard against a cropped or filtered dump producing a confident answer from missing evidence.

Cost and trade-offs against a local clone

  Browser tools (this post) git clone --depth 1 plus local tools
Setup None Network fetch and disk
Disk used None 1,812 KB for this repository, of which 304 KB is .git
Completeness Sampled (GitDiagram read 40 files) or cropped (GitIngest preview at 300k characters) Everything tracked
Privacy The repository name and content go to a third party Stays on your machine
Repeatable in CI Not shown to work (see Failure 3) Yes
Freshness A snapshot, or live through GitMCP git pull
Cost Free, with ads or sponsors Free

For this 313-file repository the clone is 1,812 KB on disk, with a 304 KB .git. The browser tools do not save you bytes at this size. They save you the decision to set anything up, which matters for a repository you will open once and does not matter for one you will work in. Timings are left out on purpose: they depend on the network and the day.

Key takeaways

  • The trick is the same in every case. Open the repository on GitHub, then retype the host. github1s.com, gitingest.com, gitdiagram.com, gitmcp.io, githubbox.com and deepwiki.com all take owner/repo after it.
  • Match the tool to the question. Reading and searching: github1s. Shape of an unfamiliar repository: GitDiagram. One-off questions to an LLM: GitIngest. Repeated questions: GitMCP. Running a JavaScript project: GitHubBox.
  • Scope before you paste. One exclude list took the test repository from 280 files and 173.5k estimated tokens to 151 files and 64.1k.
  • Verify the AI-generated views. GitDiagram read 40 of 280 files and drew a hub node the repository does not have. Use it as a table of contents and confirm in the source.
  • Know what did not work. GitHubBox showed a blank preview for a Maven project, DeepWiki had not indexed the repository and asks for an email, and GitMCP was configured from its page but not run end to end here.
  • Do not use these on private code unless cleared. The server-side tools run on someone else’s infrastructure.
  • For anything repeatable, clone. A shallow clone of this repository is 1,812 KB on disk, runs offline, and scripts cleanly.

References

  • github1s, the VS Code web viewer for GitHub repositories
  • GitIngest, which turns a repository into a prompt-ready text file
  • GitDiagram, which generates an architecture diagram and a Markdown overview
  • GitMCP, which serves a repository as a remote MCP endpoint
  • GitHubBox, which opens a repository in CodeSandbox
  • DeepWiki, which hosts generated wikis for indexed repositories
  • The test repository, rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments
  • Model Context Protocol for what an MCP server and client are

No install, no clone, and for public repositories no sign-in. They split into three jobs: read a repo (github1s), feed a repo to an LLM (GitIngest, GitMCP), and understand a repo (GitDiagram, DeepWiki). GitHubBox is the odd one out: it runs a repo, and only helps if the repo is a JavaScript project. Every screenshot in this post comes from one real repository, rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments: 280 text files, Scala and Java, Maven build. That choice exposes the limits as well as the wins. Two of the tools did not work for this repo, and the post says so and shows why. Why read a repository without cloning it A pull request link, a Stack Overflow answer or a colleague’s message lands you in a repository you have never seen. The default move is git clone, then an IDE import, then a Maven or sbt dependency download, all to answer a question like “where does this job write its output?”. For a repository you will not touch again, that is minutes of setup for a thirty-second question. A family of small sites removes the setup by taking the GitHub URL itself as input. You change github.com to another host, or put another host in front of the path, and the page you land on has done the work: an editor with search, a single text file ready to paste into a chat, a diagram, or a server your AI assistant can query. This post runs each of them, in order, on the same repository so the outputs are comparable. It is a tutorial first: each tool has numbered steps and a screenshot taken during the run. It also records where each tool stops, because “works on any repo” is only true of some of them. The test repository All runs use rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments. It is a good subject because it is awkward in the ways real repositories are: Property Value Why it matters Files 280 text files analysed by GitIngest Large enough that a naive dump is cropped Layout 34 top-level folders, 32 of them Maven modules (each has a pom.xml), one per Spark integration A diagram has to summarise, not list Languages Scala 153,704 bytes, Java 41,228, Shell 23,514, Python 5,074 (GitHub languages API) Not JavaScript, which matters for GitHubBox History 102 commits, one branch, last commit eaf9e23 Small enough to read, old enough to be unmaintained What the URL rewrite actually does None of these sites is magic. Each one is a web application that receives owner/repo in the URL, fetches the repository from GitHub on the server side (or, for github1s, in your browser), and renders a different view of it. The rewrite is the cheapest possible interface: you already have the GitHub URL, so the only thing you type is the part that changes. https://github.com/rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments | | swap the host, keep owner/repo v github1s.com /rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments -> VS Code in the browser gitingest.com /rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments -> one text file for an LLM gitdiagram.com /rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments -> architecture diagram gitmcp.io /rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments -> MCP server URL githubbox.com /rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments -> redirects to CodeSandbox deepwiki.com /rangareddy/ranga_spark_experiments -> generated wiki, if indexed All six take the same two path segments. Only the host differs, so the habit to build is: open the repository on GitHub, then retype the host. Three jobs, three places the work happens The tools differ less in what they show than in where the computation runs and what they cost you. Tool Job Where the work runs What you get Needs sign-in github1s Read and search Your browser, which loads a VS Code web build A read-only VS Code workbench No GitIngest Feed an LLM Server One text file: summary, tree, file contents No GitMCP Feed an LLM, live Server, over MCP A URL your assistant calls as tools No GitDiagram Understand Server, using an LLM A Mermaid diagram of the architecture No DeepWiki Understand Server, using an LLM A wiki, after an indexing job Email to index GitHubBox Run CodeSandbox A cloud dev environment Not to open “Needs sign-in” is for a public repository, as observed in this run. Private repositories need tokens or accounts on most of these, and none was tried here. The trade-off all six share Each tool trades privacy and completeness for speed. The server-side ones receive the repository name, and GitHubBox, GitIngest and GitDiagram each run on someone else’s infrastructure, so none of them belongs anywhere near a private repository you have not cleared. The model-backed ones (GitDiagram, DeepWiki) also summarise: they read a slice of the repository, which the sections below quantify (GitDiagram reported reading 40 source files out of 280). The alternative is the tool you already have: git clone --depth 1, then tree, rg and your IDE. It is complete, private and offline, and it costs the clone plus the import. The six tools win on the first minute and lose on everything after it. Hands-on demo: each tool, step by step, on a real repository Every step below was run on 12 November 2026 in Chrome against the repository above, signed in to nothing but GitHub. The screenshots are from those runs, unedited apart from file size. Each tool section ends with what it did not do, because that is the part the landing pages leave out.
